articles.summary: Saudi Arabia postpones big investor conference to 2027 as Iran-backed Houthis escalate attacks on kingdom  CNBCSaudi Arabia cancels 2026 ‘Davos in the Desert’ amid Houthi attacks  Al JazeeraExclusive | Wall Street Elite Can’t Decide How to RSVP to the Prince’s Big Saudi Conference  WSJSaudi Arabia Postpones Its FII Investment Event After Houthi Attacks  The New York TimesSaudi Arabia postpones its 'Davos in the Desert' conference after attacks  R...
articles.full_text:
Saudi Arabia on Monday postponed its big annual investor conference until 2027 as Iran-backed Houthi militants have escalated missile and drone attacks on the kingdom in recent weeks.
The Future Investment Initiative was originally scheduled to take place in the Saudi capital Riyadh from Oct. 26 to Oct. 29. “We will announce the new 2027 dates very soon,” the conference organizers said in a statement.
The decision to postpone the conference comes after the Houthis attacked King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Oct. 10, leaving at least 12 people dead and more than 300 injured.
Some of the biggest names in business and finance were listed as speakers for the conference. They included JPMorgan Chase’s Jamie Dimon, Goldman Sachs’ David Solomon, Blackstone’s Stephen Schwarzman, BlackRock’s Larry Fink and Citigroup’s Jane Fraser.
CNBC was told some participants and speakers had planned to travel to Saudi Arabia by flying first to Bahrain and then driving five hours to Riyadh.
Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund launched the Future Investment Initiative in 2017. The conference has played a key part in Riyadh’s plans to diversify its oil-dependent economy. Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman unveiled the ambitious megaproject NEOM at the first conference in 2017.
The decision to postpone the conference underscores the deteriorating security situation in the Middle East as the U.S-Iran war spreads across the region. Houthi militants have launched repeated waves of missile and drone strikes at Saudi Arabia since the deadly airport attack earlier this month.
The Houthis claimed on Monday to have attacked King Khalid International Airport again; Abha International Airport in southwestern Saudi Arabia, close to Yemen; Saudi Aramco facilities in Yanbu on the Red Sea Coast; the Shaybah oilfield and Saudi naval forces.
The Saudi military destroyed several drones launched at the Riyadh region on Friday and Saturday, a spokesperson for the kingdom’s armed forces said. Missiles launched over the Red Sea were also intercepted Friday including one heading toward the port city and oil terminal Yanbu, the spokesperson said.

articles.title: How could Israel most effectively support Saudi Arabia against the Houthis? - The Jerusalem Post
articles.summary: How could Israel most effectively support Saudi Arabia against the Houthis?  The Jerusalem Post
articles.full_text:
There is increased discussion about how Israel might help Saudi Arabia against the Iranian-backed Houthis. How might such help take shape, and what might be most effective?
This comes amid wider questions about whether Saudi Arabia will join the Abraham Accords. Questions about this have come up since the accords began in 2020. So far, Riyadh has taken a wait-and-see approach, preferring that Israel make positive moves on the Palestinian issue.
Now, US President Donald Trump has said that Saudi Arabia may be accepting help from Israel. Asked about whether he thought Saudi Arabia might normalize ties with Israel, he said, “I think they will. Israel’s been very helpful to Saudi Arabia.” The comments were made days after Saudi Arabia appeared to downplay whether Israel would support them.
The context for this latest development is the Houthis’ increased attacks on Saudi Arabia. America has not joined the fighting but may be supporting the Saudis in various ways, such as via intelligence.
The US has so far chosen not to join strikes on the Houthis. The Trump administration carried out strikes on the Houthis in March and April 2025. The administration eventually concluded that it was better to do a deal with the Houthis than continue strikes.
On Sunday, Walla had a piece by Amir Bohbot, asking whether Israeli aid to Saudi Arabia would be an opportunity or a potential powder keg.
“Security sources confirmed to Walla that the quality of Israeli intelligence is improving, but at the same time the Houthis are causing heavy damage. The security establishment is aware that there is an opportunity to strengthen relations, but is not addressing the issue for fear of inflaming the situation,” Bohbot reported.
The Turkish pro-government media outlet Anadolu Agency noted on October 13 that “Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has rejected an Israeli push to join the military campaign against Yemen’s Houthi group, despite efforts to secure Riyadh’s approval through US mediation.”
Anadolu Agency said it based this on a report in Haaretz. “Another source familiar with the matter said Israel hoped military cooperation with Saudi Arabia would strengthen bilateral ties and pave the way for a future normalization agreement,” the report said. “There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities on the report.”
Saudi Arabia needs Israeli aerial defense systems
Ynet noted on Sunday, in a piece by Ron Ben-Yishai, that “the Saudis urgently need early-warning radar systems and air defense batteries capable of countering different types of aerial threats, including Iron Dome, David’s Sling, and even Arrow 2 interceptors.”
“The Houthis are attacking Saudi Arabia with ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and explosive-laden drones, requiring a combination of defensive capabilities,” he added.
This analysis noted that “Trump sees a chance to revive Saudi-Israel normalization as the Houthis strike Riyadh; Israel is sharing intelligence, but Riyadh’s demand for Palestinian statehood talks and Israel’s need for its own defenses make a deal far from certain.”
It also added that Trump may see an “opportunity for greater Israeli assistance, potentially generating enough goodwill in Riyadh to persuade the Saudis to abandon their longstanding condition for normalization: negotiations with the Palestinians toward a two-state solution. For now, however, there is good reason to doubt that Trump’s comments signal a meaningful breakthrough in Israeli-Saudi relations.”
Walla noted that “security sources confirmed that as time goes by, the contribution of Israeli intelligence is increasing, with the Houthis in the background causing heavy damage to the Saudis throughout the country.”
The report goes on to say that “as first published in Walla, the IDF is assisting Saudi Arabia on the intelligence front in the fight against the Houthis in aspects of warning, target banking, and building a situational picture.”
“Israel sees this as a positive process that will intensify once the US decides how it will decide on the Iranian issue,” it said.
America, Walla said, is facing this dilemma: “If the US attacks Iran, the latter may attack the countries of the region, including Israel. If America continues with the economic sanctions (there is a slim chance of a political agreement without further conflict), this could also lead to escalation in the region.”
Houthis targeted shipping they claimed was linked to Israel after Oct. 7
The overall story now points to potential increased Israeli involvement and support. It’s worth noting that the Houthis began attacks on Israel soon after October 7. The Houthis began by attacking ships they claimed were linked to Israel.
The Iranian-backed group said that it was targeting Israeli ships and vessels linked to Israel, although many of the ships attacked had no direct Israeli ownership or operational connection.
One of the most prominent incidents occurred on November 19, 2023, when Houthi forces seized the Galaxy Leader, a vehicle carrier, in the Red Sea.
Armed men boarded the ship from a helicopter and diverted it to Yemen. A Japanese company operated the vessel and, through its ownership structure, was linked to Israeli businessman Abraham Ungar. None of its 25 crew members were Israeli nationals. They remained detained until January 2025, when the Houthis released them following the Gaza ceasefire agreement.
The seizure marked the beginning of a wider campaign against international shipping. The Houthis subsequently expanded their declared targets to include vessels traveling to Israeli ports and ships associated with American and British interests.
The Houthis also carried out ballistic missile attacks on Israel. Israel responded by striking dozens of Houthi targets in 2025. This shows that Israel has already launched a campaign against the Houthis. The US has also carried out a campaign.
Notably, Saudi Arabia has fought the Houthis since 2015. That means that all the players know the Houthi threat and capabilities. The Saudis have worked with Egypt, the UAE, and others in the past against the Houthis.
It appears that Riyadh will work again with Egypt and the UAE. Israel has ties with the UAE and Egypt via peace treaties. Israel also already works closely with the US Central Command.
Any cooperation against the Houthis can strengthen regional defense ties and infrastructure. This helps defend against Iranian-backed threats and Iran’s direct threats. For instance, when Iran carried out large missile attacks on Israel in 2024, many countries cooperated against the threat.

articles.title: Saudi-Iran Talks: Why No Deal Can Stop the Houthis - https://houseofsaud.com/
articles.summary: Saudi-Iran Talks: Why No Deal Can Stop the Houthis  https://houseofsaud.com/
articles.full_text:
RIYADH — Saudi Arabia accepted a phone call from Iran on 11 October while Houthi missiles were still hitting Saudi airports and oil infrastructure. The call did not stop the next strike, or the one after that. It could not have. Iran is the interlocutor, but the Houthis are the ones firing, and no agreement between Riyadh and Tehran can bind a group that Tehran itself cannot compel.
That is the structural problem at the centre of every diplomatic effort now underway. The kingdom proposed talks in Oman in July; the Houthis refused. Iran offered to mediate; Saudi Arabia said it had not asked. Araghchi offered “any form of support” to start dialogue; Krimly accused Iran of arming the group it offered to restrain. Each move generated a headline. None generated a mechanism that connects a signature in a foreign ministry to a ceasefire on the ground.
Four matters are at issue: the principal-agent gap that makes Saudi-Iran diplomacy structurally unenforceable, the minimum asks each side has placed on the table, the precedent — or lack of it — for the arrangement Iran is proposing, and what Riyadh’s decision to talk at all signals to Washington, Tehran, and the Houthis themselves.
The Call That Changed Nothing
On 11 October, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi called Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan — their first publicly reported contact since the Houthis escalated attacks on the kingdom. Saudi state media confirmed the call took place, according to Al Jazeera. Araghchi told Faisal that “insisting on a military approach and disregarding a political solution would only further complicate the situation,” according to the same report.
The timing was not incidental. The day before, a Houthi strike on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh killed 13 people and wounded between 308 and 309 others, according to Al Jazeera and the BBC. An Indian national’s death raised the initial toll of 12 to 13, the BBC reported on 11 October. The airport remained closed. A US citizen was among the dead, Secretary of State Marco Rubio confirmed on CBS News.
The call produced no ceasefire, no joint statement, and no follow-up meeting. By 14 October, Reuters and AP reported that a Houthi strike had caused a fire “spreading across several floors” of Aramco’s Dhahran headquarters, damaging offices including the CEO’s. The Saudi energy ministry described only “a limited fire at an administrative building” with no deaths or injuries at the site. Saudi Civil Defence reported four people injured in Riyadh from debris of intercepted missiles the same day.
Iran’s FM spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei repeated the mediation offer at a Monday briefing: “We do not want hostilities to continue between two Muslim countries,” according to BERNAMA and Al Jazeera. As of 17 October, Araghchi confirmed that Saudi Arabia had not responded to the mediation offer, Free Malaysia Today reported.
What Did Iran Actually Offer?
Iran’s offer, stripped of its diplomatic framing, amounts to this: Tehran will talk to the Houthis on Riyadh’s behalf and “provide any form of support” to start a Saudi-Houthi dialogue, as Araghchi put it on 11 October, according to Al Jazeera. On 17 October he added that Iran supports “an inclusive and comprehensive political process as the only practical and sustainable way to resolve the issue,” and offered what amounted to a threat dressed as philosophy: “either we build security together, or we will endure insecurity together,” Free Malaysia Today reported.
The language matters. “Inclusive and comprehensive” ties Yemen to the wider US-Iran confrontation rather than isolating it as a discrete ceasefire. Iran is not offering to stop the Houthis. It is offering to be the party through which any stop must pass — positioning itself, as Negar Mortazavi of the Center for International Policy told Al Jazeera, “as an indispensable party to a broader regional settlement.”
Tehran simultaneously denied involvement in the Houthi attacks. On 16 October, Iran rejected Saudi accusations of encouraging the escalation, according to CBS News. The two positions — denial of involvement and an offer to mediate the group Iran claims not to control — coexist without embarrassment. They are, in diplomatic terms, features rather than contradictions. A state that admits command authority over a proxy has legal exposure under international law. A state that claims mere influence can offer mediation without conceding liability.
The internationally recognised Yemeni foreign minister publicly criticised Iran’s mediation offer on 17 October, CBS News reported — a signal that Sanaa’s legitimate government does not want Tehran granted a mediator role, and an indication of how many parties hold veto power over any arrangement.
The Principal-Agent Gap
The core problem is not whether Iran wants to help. It is whether Iran can deliver what it promises. Every major analyst who has studied the Iran-Houthi relationship describes Tehran as a supplier and influencer, not a command authority.
Andreas Krieg of King’s College London told Al Jazeera that “Ansar Allah is not simply an Iranian proxy awaiting instructions.” Iran “can facilitate talks and potentially influence the intensity of escalation,” he said — language that concedes influence while denying control. Ali Alfoneh of the Arab Gulf States Institute in Washington wrote that Iran needed “considerable time and effort” to persuade the Houthis to act against Saudi Arabia, and that “one could argue that, in the end, Ansarullah acted more out of self-interest than to accommodate Tehran,” according to the Christian Science Monitor.
The evidence supports this reading. The Houthis halted Red Sea attacks on Israeli-linked shipping after the October 2025 Gaza ceasefire without an apparent Iranian directive. They then stayed on the sidelines for months after the 28 February US-Israeli strikes on Iran — again without visible instruction from Tehran.
Laurent Bonnefoy of CNRS/Sciences Po noted that Houthi leaders “appeared to disregard” reports that Iran asked them in July 2026 to close Bab el-Mandeb, according to Asia Times. The IRGC-linked Tasnim news agency urged Ansarullah in early September to see itself as part of a larger Axis system — which, as the Christian Science Monitor observed, suggests the group was not already integrated into one.
Saudi Arabia proposed a meeting in Oman in July 2026 to end the escalation. The Houthis refused, according to AP. Iran was not part of that channel. The refusal came from the actor, not the patron.
This is the gap that no phone call can close. A ceasefire requires enforcement. Enforcement requires command authority. Iran has influence. The distance between influence and authority is the distance between a diplomatic communiqué and a grounded missile.
Why the Beijing Deal Contained No Houthi Commitment
The 2023 Beijing agreement, which restored Saudi-Iranian diplomatic ties and reopened embassies, is frequently cited as a precedent for what diplomacy might achieve. It is a poor one. The deal contained no published Yemen-specific commitment, according to the Christian Science Monitor. A Saudi official told the Monitor at the time that the agreement produced “concrete commitments” on Yemen but would not disclose them. US envoy Tim Lenderking framed stopping arms smuggling as a condition, not an agreed term.
The adversary confirmation came in September 2026. At the margin of the UN General Assembly on 22 September, IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebi said plainly: “The issue of Yemen was not on the agenda of the previous agreement.” He went further. Iran, he said, now demands “that the lifting of the blockade on Yemen be included in the agreement,” according to Middle East Eye. Yemen had not been part of the deal. It was now a new demand.
This is a significant admission. It means that when Iran signed the Beijing deal in 2023, it signed no Houthi-restraint commitment. Iran armed the war it offered to mediate — the pattern visible in the current crisis — was already embedded in the only major Saudi-Iran agreement of the past decade. The deal restored embassies. It did not restrain proxies. The distinction matters because anyone proposing a second Beijing-style agreement must explain what the first one actually bound Iran to do about Yemen. The answer, by Iran’s own account, is nothing.
What Does Each Side Want?
Saudi Arabia’s implied minimum is verifiable Iranian weapons restraint — not promises. The Houthis demand the lifting of the blockade on Houthi-controlled Yemen. Iran’s own price sits above both: sanctions relief, Hormuz access, and the release of billions in frozen US-held assets. No party has offered the concession the other requires to move.
Saudi Arabia has not publicly stated its minimum ask from Iran. It has, however, stated what it believes Iran is doing. Deputy FM Rayed Krimly, speaking at a briefing in Cairo on 15 October, accused Iran of encouraging Houthi escalation and continuing to arm the group in violation of UN Security Council resolutions, per AP — the full set of charges is detailed in the section below.
The implied Saudi minimum is verifiable restraint — a mechanism by which Iran demonstrates, not merely promises, that weapons transfers and operational support to the Houthis have ceased. Riyadh wants to talk to the Houthis directly, through Oman, not through Tehran.
The Houthi minimum is less ambiguous. Mohebi’s September statement at the UN — demanding the lifting of the blockade on Houthi-controlled Yemen — represents the price Iran has placed on the table on behalf of its ally. Military spokesperson Yahya Saree told aviation companies, workers and travellers to avoid Saudi airports and airspace “except those serving Mecca and Medina,” according to Middle East Eye. The exemption for the holy cities is the Houthis’ own red line — religious legitimacy they cannot afford to cross. Everything else, from Riyadh’s airport to Aramco’s headquarters, remains a target.

articles.summary: Saudi Arabia sends skyscraper employees home amid Houthi threats  DW.com
articles.full_text:
The Kingdom Center skyscraper in Riyadh told people employed there to work from home due to possible attacks by Yemen's Houthi rebels.
The 99-storey tower is one of Saudi Arabia's tallest buildings.
Kingdom Center made working from home "mandatory" with no reason given. The new order is effective immediately and will be in power until further notice, the building's management told tenants, AFP reported.
Among the building's tenants are important financial institutions such as the International Monetary Fund, as well as wealth management company Merril Lynch.
At the building's foot is a shopping center, which will remain open for now.
Attacks increase
Studies in schools across Saudi capital Riyadh and the surrounding areas will take place online for a second week, with the city's King Khalid International Airport still being closed after a Houthi attack resulted in 13 casualties.
The conflict between the Saudi-led coalition and Iran-backed Islamist group Houthis has continued to escalate, with the coalition reporting its first military deaths since the escalation's beginning.
Two helicopter pilots were killed near the Yemen border due to a "technical malfunction," the coalition said, with the Houthis earlier announcing the downing of an Apache helicopter "belonging to the Saudi enemy," the group said.
Conflict flares up again
On the Saudi side, two drones were intercepted over Riyadh overnight, with a third being shot down over the country's Eastern Province, a known oil-rich area, according to the authorities in the country.
Two ballistic missiles were also intercepted in Saudi Arabia's south.
The two sides have been confronting each other on various intensities over the past decade. After a four-year ceasefire, the conflict between the two sides saw an escalation after the Yemen-based Islamist militia took over strategic territory along the Red Sea coast last month.
The Houthis have targeted oil facilities, tankers and Riyadh's international airport, with the coalition carrying out strikes on Houthi areas.

articles.title: Why Saudi Arabia has failed to defeat the Houthis - نون بوست
articles.summary: Why Saudi Arabia has failed to defeat the Houthis  نون بوست
articles.full_text:
هذا التقرير متاح أيضًا بـ العربية
Saudi Arabia entered the war in Yemen in 2015 with overwhelming military superiority, an advanced arsenal of fighter jets, missiles and air defence systems, and leadership of a regional coalition seeking to retake the capital, Sanaa, and end Houthi control over state institutions. But after more than 11 years of military operations, the group remains entrenched in its main strongholds and has developed missile capabilities that can threaten vital facilities inside the kingdom.
The Saudi campaign’s failure stems from a misreading of the war and a heavy reliance on air strikes against a group experienced in mountain warfare and attritional conflict. The Houthis also drew on the Yemeni army’s arsenal and Iranian support to build a growing military force, while divisions and Saudi-Emirati rivalry weakened the Yemeni forces opposing them and hampered efforts to retake Houthi-held areas.
With large-scale clashes resuming in 2026, the cost of any new Saudi attempt to secure a military victory has risen as the Houthis have expanded their attacks on oil facilities, airports and economic infrastructure. Retaking Sanaa would also require an extensive ground campaign, alongside security and political arrangements that would prevent the group from returning to the battlefield. Why have the Houthis not been defeated after so many years, and what still prevents Riyadh from winning the war militarily?
Misreading the war and relying too heavily on air power
The Saudi campaign’s problems began with its initial assessment of the war. Riyadh entered the conflict on 26 March 2015 expecting a swift victory through intensive air strikes that would pave the way for forces loyal to the Yemeni government to retake Sanaa. The Houthis had seized the capital in September 2014 before expanding south with support from military units loyal to former Yemeni president Ali Abdullah Saleh.
Saudi Arabia enjoyed overwhelming superiority in fighter jets, long-range munitions, reconnaissance and military logistics. Its military spending reflected that advantage, reaching about $83.2 billion in 2025, according to estimates published by the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute on 27 April 2026. This placed the kingdom eighth worldwide and first in the Middle East.
The coalition made extensive use of this superiority. The Yemen Data Project, an independent initiative that monitors air operations, documented 25,054 air strikes by the Saudi- and UAE-led coalition between March 2015 and March 2022.
But Yemen’s geography favoured the Houthis’ defence, particularly in the northern and western highlands around Sanaa and Saada, with their steep mountain ranges, valleys and narrow passes. This terrain lends itself to ambushes and fortified positions, provides cover for weapons depots and allows fighters to move in small groups that are difficult to detect and target.
Since 2004, the Houthis have gained extensive experience in guerrilla warfare. They rely on small units bound by social and tribal ties, using ambushes, sniping, mines and local knowledge of mountain passes to make their positions difficult for attacking forces to detect and capture.
In a study published by Cambridge University Press in late 2021, military researcher Ralph Shield concluded that Saudi air power had helped impede Houthi advances and prevent the group from taking control of all of Yemen. He found that it achieved better results when supporting ground forces, while strategies involving bombing, blockade and the targeting of leaders faced major difficulties in subduing the group and forcing it to surrender.
The limits of that superiority became clear in the battle of Marib in 2021, when the Houthis launched a major offensive on the province east of Sanaa, the internationally recognised government’s most prominent stronghold in northern Yemen. The coalition deployed military reinforcements and intensified air strikes to support government forces, helping to slow the Houthi advance. Fighting nevertheless continued for months without a decisive outcome.
In January 2022, the Giants Brigades, Yemeni military formations backed by the UAE, made rapid gains in Shabwa province and Marib’s Harib district. They benefited from training, weapons, organisation and air support, underscoring the importance of ground forces capable of capitalising on air strikes to seize and hold positions.
Targeting and intelligence failures further complicated the campaign. A Reuters investigation published on 19 April 2016 pointed to excessive reliance, at some stages of the operations, on information supplied by local Yemeni parties.
The investigation cited a 2010 US diplomatic cable documenting the cancellation of a Saudi strike after it emerged that the target supplied by the Yemeni authorities was the headquarters of a military commander at odds with former president Ali Abdullah Saleh. The incident highlighted the risks of relying on intelligence from parties involved in local conflicts.
Air strikes that caused civilian casualties also drew mounting international criticism. In September 2021, the UN Human Rights Council’s Group of Eminent International and Regional Experts announced that, since 2018, it had investigated about 30 coalition strikes that caused civilian deaths and injuries. In specific cases, it found failures concerning distinction, proportionality and the precautions required during attacks. The coalition rejected some of those findings and criticised the investigations’ methodology.
Political and human rights pressure also helped change the level of western support for the operations. The US halted aerial refuelling for coalition aircraft in 2018. In February 2021, the administration of former US president Joe Biden announced an end to support for offensive operations linked to the war. Restrictions on offensive weapons sales to Saudi Arabia were subsequently lifted in 2024.
The Houthis’ growing strength and ability to absorb losses
The Houthis withstood the Saudi campaign thanks to their arsenal of heavy weapons, military expertise and institutions for financing and recruitment. Access to Yemeni army weapons, their alliance with former president Ali Abdullah Saleh and, later, Iranian support in developing missiles and drones strengthened their ability to absorb losses and continue fighting.
After the Houthis took control of Sanaa in 2014, their alliance with Saleh gave them access to army stockpiles and military systems, as well as the expertise of officers, engineers and technicians in the armed forces. Security and military units loyal to the former president continued fighting alongside them during the early years of the Saudi intervention.
The weapons seized by the Houthis included tanks, artillery, ballistic missiles and air defence systems. In June 2015, forces allied with them launched a Scud ballistic missile towards Saudi Arabia. The Houthis’ relationship with Saleh later unravelled and ended with his killing in December 2017. By then, the group had already absorbed a large share of the military and security capabilities associated with him.
Iranian support subsequently helped the Houthis develop their weaponry. Reports issued by the US Defense Intelligence Agency in 2024 documented that support, identifying technical similarities between Iranian systems and the missiles and drones used by the group, as well as components and weapons seized in shipments bound for Yemen.
Iranian assistance included the transfer of equipment, technology and expertise for assembling and operating missiles and drones, alongside training and the development of targeting, navigation and air defence capabilities. This helped the Houthis extend the range of their attacks and deploy more sophisticated systems.
On 15 October 2026, Andreas Krieg, a professor of security studies at King’s College London, explained that members of Iran’s Revolutionary Guard and Lebanon’s Hezbollah had helped the Houthis acquire technical knowledge of missiles and drones. He said former Yemeni military engineers and locally trained technicians had also helped develop this expertise within the group.
An October 2026 field study by the UK-based Conflict Armament Research also confirmed that the Houthis were seeking to manufacture parts for medium-range ballistic missiles inspired by Iran’s Kheibar Shekan system. Researchers examined components, testing tools and materials linked to solid-fuel engines seized in shipments bound for the group. Shipping documents identified a Chinese supplier of some components, indicating that supply networks were expanding.
Alongside developing their weaponry, the Houthis expanded their ranks. A 2024 report by the UN Panel of Experts estimated that the number of fighters affiliated with the group had risen from about 30,000 in 2015 to 350,000.
The UN also documented the use of schools, summer centres, incentives and social pressure to recruit children and young people. Its 2025 annual report on children and armed conflict verified the recruitment and use of 127 children by the Houthis, warning that restrictions on access to some areas hindered efforts to document all cases.
The Houthis used their control over state institutions to collect taxes, customs duties, fees and levies, alongside revenues from the telecommunications, fuel and commercial sectors. In its 2024 report, the UN Panel of Experts estimated that the revenues the group collected and controlled during 2023 totalled about 3.392 trillion Yemeni rials, or about $6.4 billion.
Those revenues included about 300 billion rials from land collection points. The panel said some of those proceeds were used to pay fighters’ salaries and finance military activities.

articles.title: Houthi ballistic missile strike kills at least 53 Yemen govt troops
articles.summary: Houthi rebels killed at least 53 Yemeni government soldiers in a ballistic missile strike on a military camp Monday, one of the deadliest attacks since fighting surged this summer,...
articles.full_text:
Houthi rebels killed at least 53 Yemeni government soldiers in a ballistic missile strike on a military camp Monday, one of the deadliest attacks since fighting surged this summer, military officials said.
The attack wounded an additional 200 recruits at the military camp in the southern province of Shabwa, the provincial government there said. The rebels acknowledged targeting the camp.
The fighting between the Houthis and Yemen’s Saudi-backed government forces is a widening front in the Iran war that began in February. The escalation shattered a 2022 cease-fire deal that largely stopped fighting in Yemen’s civil war.
The Houthis have put their growing military capabilities on display on multiple fronts in recent weeks, repeatedly striking Saudi Arabia’s main international airport hundreds of kilometers away and seizing territory inside Yemen near a key shipping chokepoint.
Iran and its allies in Lebanon and Iraq provide expertise, training and sophisticated weapons to the Houthis, according to U.N. and other experts. Iran denies arming the Houthis, which would violate a U.N. embargo.
The provincial government in Shabwa said in a statement that the death toll is preliminary and may rise. It said the recruits were receiving training to be part of internal security forces.
"This bloody, treacherous attack targeted new recruits in the training and preparation phase and is considered an extremely critical military escalation and a blatant aggression on the security and stability of Shabwa province," the statement said.
It called on Yemen’s president, the Saudi-led coalition and the government to expedite air defense and early warning systems to reinforce Shabwa’s capabilities.
The head of Yemen's ruling Presidential Leadership Council, Rashad al-Alimi, promised a "firm response" and said the attack reflects the Houthis' "approach of resorting to cowardly terrorist attacks whenever they face pressures or their Iranian-backed sabotage plots falter."
One Yemeni military official said the missiles struck while recruits were lining up in formation for a training session. The official spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to talk to the media.
On Sunday, an airstrike blamed on Saudi-led forces killed at least nine people in Yemen’s rebel-held northern province of Saada, the Houthi-run Health Ministry said. Five children and two women were killed in the attack, one of several that killed or wounded more than 30 people over the weekend, according to the rebels.
There was no immediate comment from Saudi Arabia.
The Houthis, a Shiite religious and political movement rooted in northern Yemen, are increasingly attacking Saudi Arabia because it supports Yemen’s internationally recognized government in the civil war. The Sunni kingdom, which has long feared the emergence of a well-armed ally of Shiite Iran on its border, joined the war in 2015 after the rebels seized much of northern Yemen, including the capital, Sanaa.
The rebels have been targeting Saudi airports and oil and military facilities. The headquarters of Saudi oil giant Aramco has been struck as well in a blow to the world’s top oil exporter.
The rebels also recently seized more territory along Yemen’s Red Sea coast and near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a crucial shipping alternative to the Strait of Hormuz.

articles.summary: SAMA Governor: Saudi Infrastructure Sustains Oil Supplies, Regional Trade Amid Conflict  ASHARQ AL-AWSAT English
articles.full_text:
Saudi Arabia’s diversified energy infrastructure and logistics networks have enabled the Kingdom to maintain oil supplies and regional trade despite the widening economic fallout from the Middle East conflict, said Saudi Central Bank (SAMA) Governor Ayman Al-Sayari.
Addressing the International Monetary and Financial Committee (IMFC) of the International Monetary Fund in Bangkok, chaired by Saudi Finance Minister Mohammed Al-Jadaan, Al-Sayari highlighted the Kingdom’s ability to withstand the crisis, supported by prudent policies, substantial financial and nonfinancial buffers, and a well-capitalized banking sector.
He stressed Saudi Arabia’s commitment to supporting economic activity and preserving monetary and financial stability without compromising fiscal sustainability.
Al-Sayari stressed that energy security depended not only on the availability of supplies but also on their reliable and affordable delivery to international markets.
He called for sustained investment throughout the energy supply chain, from production and refining to storage and diversified transport routes, as well as across all energy sources, including oil and gas.
The conflict’s initial impact, concentrated in energy markets and major shipping corridors, had gradually spread to trade, transportation, inflation, financing conditions and investor confidence.
Disruptions had also extended beyond crude oil and natural gas to refined petroleum products, particularly transportation fuels, as well as fertilizers and essential production inputs, increasing price pressures and threatening food security and production.
While rerouting supplies and drawing down inventories had helped cushion the immediate shock, those measures had reduced the capacity to absorb further disruptions, Al-Sayari cautioned.
Banking sector withstands shocks
Turning to the domestic economy, Al-Sayari highlighted the resilience of Saudi banks, whose capital and liquidity positions remain robust, with financial soundness indicators among the strongest in the region.
He attributed the Kingdom’s ability to preserve domestic stability to decades of prudent economic management, effective risk management and strategic investment, explaining that its extensive energy and logistics infrastructure had also helped maintain oil supplies and regional commerce and mitigate the impact of disruptions in global energy markets.
He underlined that Saudi Arabia would continue adjusting its response as the conflict evolved, preserving room to address further developments while maintaining fiscal discipline.
Vision 2030 strengthens economic foundations
Al-Sayari said Saudi Vision 2030, now entering its tenth year, had reinforced the Kingdom’s economic foundations by expanding non-oil activity, increasing private sector participation and strengthening institutions and reform implementation.
He underlined the government’s commitment to productivity-enhancing reforms, greater private investment opportunities, more efficient public spending and sound public finances.
The next phase would focus on further diversification, deeper financial markets and human capital development, alongside improvements in infrastructure and institutional capacity to support sustainable and inclusive growth.
IMF urged to implement institutional reforms
On international cooperation, Al-Sayari called on the IMF to prioritize the implementation of recently reviewed institutional reforms covering economic surveillance, program design and conditionality, financial sector assessments and the debt sustainability framework for low-income countries.
Fund-supported programs should reflect individual countries’ circumstances, needs and capacity to implement reforms with conditions focused on measures essential to their success, he remarked.
He also advocated closer coordination between surveillance, lending and technical assistance, as well as timely and orderly resolution of unsustainable debt and stronger cooperation among creditors.
Al-Sayari reiterated Saudi Arabia’s support for IMF capacity development, including its $279 million pledge and backing for the Fund’s regional office in Riyadh.
He also drew attention to risks stemming from volatile capital flows, rising sovereign bond yields and the expanding role of nonbank financial institutions.
Artificial intelligence and stablecoins presented implications for both productivity and financial stability, underscoring the importance of strengthening analysis and oversight to address emerging risks, he noted.

Riyadh’s iconic Kingdom Centre skyscraper ordered office tenants to work remotely Sunday following repeated Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, as the Saudi-led coalition said two pilots were killed in a crash near the Yemen border.
The 99-story building mandated remote working until further notice. Management gave no reason for the order, but it followed a major Houthi attack on Riyadh's international airport a week earlier that killed 13 people.
The Saudi-led coalition's more than decadelong war with the Iran-backed Houthis has reignited, with both sides reporting regular attacks.
Tenants of the Kingdom Centre, which towers over central Riyadh, include financial services giant Merrill Lynch, management consultancy McKinsey and the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
"Please be advised that remote working arrangements are mandatory for all office employees at Kingdom Centre, effective immediately and until further notice," the building's management said in an email.
"Kindly refrain from attending the offices during this period," it added. The mall at the building's foot remains open.
The order comes as schools recently extended remote learning and Riyadh's international airport remains closed following last week's attack.
The order came after the coalition announced the deaths of two helicopter pilots in Najran near the Yemen border, blaming a "technical malfunction." This contradicted Houthi claims that they shot down an Apache helicopter in the area.
"An AH-6i reconnaissance helicopter belonging to the Ministry of National Guard crashed inside Saudi territory in Najran region due to a technical malfunction," coalition spokesperson Turki al-Malki said, according to the Saudi Press Agency.
"The accident resulted in the martyrdom of its aircrew, consisting of two officers."
Late Saturday, Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree said the group had "downed an Apache helicopter belonging to the Saudi enemy" in the same area.
After an uneasy, four-year truce, Yemen's conflict has surged back to life and intensified. The Houthis seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast last month.
The Houthis have hit Saudi targets including tankers in the Red Sea, oil facilities and Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport.
The Saudi-led coalition backing the internationally recognized government has launched repeated air raids on Houthi territory.
The coalition said overnight it intercepted two drones in the Riyadh area and a third over the Eastern province. Saudi authorities had earlier issued a threat alert in the capital.
The coalition also said it intercepted two ballistic missiles in the kingdom's south.
On Saturday, the Houthis reported that Saudi strikes killed 12 people in Yemen, including three children.
The Houthis have declared a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia and captured territory around the Bab el-Mandeb strait, a Red Sea choke point and vital export route for Saudi oil.
The Red Sea is a key shipping route, connecting Asia with Europe via Egypt's Suez Canal.
On Sunday, Egypt's parliament will hold an emergency session after President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi asked lawmakers to authorize support to defend Saudi Arabia against Houthi attacks.
El-Sissi said he was willing to "carry out any measure to protect" Saudi Arabia if its leaders requested it.
"I'm not talking about fighting anyone or attacking anyone," he said Saturday. "We are speaking only about defense."

articles.title: Morocco And Israel: The Multi-Tiered Relationship From History To The Abraham Accords - Analysis - Eurasia Review
articles.summary: Morocco And Israel: The Multi-Tiered Relationship From History To The Abraham Accords - Analysis  Eurasia Review
articles.full_text:
Key Takeaways:
- The essay argues that Morocco–Israel relations form a six-tier structure—history, conviviality, religious complicity, sincerity, mutual interest, and the Abraham Accords—whose lower layers of long-term Jewish presence and shared life give the 2020 normalization and 2026 embassy upgrade a depth that has allowed the relationship to survive repeated crises.
- It identifies the core vulnerability as an asymmetry: the upper tiers that carry the greatest strategic weight, especially the Accords and defense cooperation, enjoy the weakest popular legitimacy, as Arab Barometer data show support for normalization falling to 13 percent after October 2023.
- The author concludes that the relationship’s resilience depends on protecting the socially embedded lower tiers while converting elite strategic benefits into broader societal gains and keeping the Palestinian question visible.
This essay analyzes the relationship between Morocco and Israel as a stratified structure of six interlocking tiers: history, conviviality, religious complicity, sincerity, mutual interest and well-being, and the Abraham Accords. Rather than treating the diplomatic normalization of December 2020 as the origin of the relationship, the essay situates it at the summit of a deeper edifice whose lower tiers—two and a half millennia of Jewish presence in the Maghrib, shared urban and rural life, intertwined devotional practice, and a royal discourse of protection—supply the symbolic and social capital on which the upper tiers draw. Drawing on historiography, anthropology, constitutional texts, diplomatic documents, public-opinion data, and developments through October 2026, including the upgrade to full embassies announced in September 2026 and Israel’s first national pavilion at the Marrakech Air Show, the essay advances a “layered resilience” thesis: the relationship has survived ruptures because its tiers operate on different temporalities and carry different legitimacies. It also identifies the relationship’s principal vulnerability, an asymmetry between the tier with the greatest strategic weight, which has the weakest popular legitimacy, and the tiers with the deepest social legitimacy, which are the least institutionalized.
Introduction
The proposition that Morocco and Israel share an unbroken relationship of two and a half thousand years is at once a historical claim, a political slogan, and an invitation to analysis. As history, it compresses a long and discontinuous record of Jewish presence in the western Maghrib, attested archaeologically in the Roman period and traditionally traced to Phoenician-era commerce (Gottreich, 2020; Hirschberg, 1974; Laskier, 1994). As slogan, it has been mobilized by the Moroccan monarchy, by Israeli diplomats, and by the Moroccan Jewish diaspora to present the diplomatic normalization announced on 10 December 2020 not as a novelty but as a restoration (Ben-Layashi & Maddy-Weitzman, 2010; Gulf News, 2020). As an invitation to analysis, it raises a question the slogan leaves open: of what, exactly, is the relationship composed, and why has it survived circumstances—colonial domination, mass emigration, successive Arab–Israeli wars, the closure of the liaison offices in 2000, and the devastation of Gaza after October 2023—that have ended lesser ties?
This essay answers that question by proposing that the relationship is not a single bond but a stack of six tiers, each with its own carriers, its own temporality, and its own source of legitimacy. The first tier is history: the long presence of Jews in Morocco and the political arrangements that governed it. The second is conviviality: the daily practice of shared space, language, commerce, and sociability between Muslims and Jews. The third is religious complicity, by which is meant the affinity, and at times the genuine collusion, between Moroccan Muslim and Jewish religiosity, expressed in shared saints, shared pilgrimage, and a common Abrahamic grammar. The fourth is sincerity: the extent to which the professed attachments of the monarchy, of Moroccan Jews at home and abroad, of Moroccan Muslim society, and of Israel are authentic rather than instrumental. The fifth is mutual interest and well-being: the security, economic, technological, and societal benefits that both states expect from cooperation. The sixth and uppermost is the Abraham Accords, the legal-diplomatic framework within which the relationship was resumed in December 2020 and is being institutionalized in 2026.
The argument developed here is that the six tiers differ in what Fernand Braudel (1958) called their duration. The lower tiers belong to the long term; the upper tiers belong to the conjuncture and the event. Because the lower tiers change slowly, they have repeatedly absorbed shocks that would otherwise have severed the relationship, and they furnish the Moroccan state with a vocabulary of continuity that makes each diplomatic step—liaison offices in 1994, normalization in 2020, embassies in 2026—appear as a return rather than a rupture (Chtatou, 2021c; Pennell, 2000). This is the thesis of layered resilience. Its corollary is a warning: the upper tiers carry the greatest strategic weight but the thinnest popular legitimacy, as survey evidence collected by the Arab Barometer since 2021 shows (Hespress English, 2025; Morocco World News, 2022). The tiers with the deepest social legitimacy, by contrast, are the least institutionalized and the most exposed to demographic erosion, since the Jewish population of Morocco has fallen from a quarter of a million in the late 1940s to a few thousand today (Laskier, 1994).
The essay is analytical and interpretive. It triangulates three bodies of evidence: the historiography of Moroccan Jewry and of Moroccan–Israeli diplomacy; anthropological and memory studies of Muslim–Jewish coexistence; and primary and contemporary documentary sources, including the 2011 Constitution, United Nations Security Council Resolution 2797 (2025), diplomatic communiqués, and polling data (Kingdom of Morocco, 2011; United Nations Security Council, 2025). It privileges the Moroccan vantage point without neglecting Israeli and American perspectives, and it extends to developments of September and October 2026. Each of the six sections that follow defines its tier, reviews the evidence, and identifies the tier’s contribution to the whole and its characteristic fragility. A discussion section then examines the interaction among the tiers, and a conclusion draws out implications for scholarship and policy.
Conceptual Framework: Why Tiers, and What the Tiers Are Not
A stratified model is preferable to a linear narrative for three reasons. First, the evidence for Moroccan–Jewish history is discontinuous: golden ages and persecutions, protection and humiliation, intimacy and segregation coexisted, sometimes in the same city and the same decade (Cohen, 1994; Lewis, 1984; Stillman, 1979). A linear account must choose between nostalgia and grievance; a stratified account can hold both, assigning each to the tier where it belongs. Second, the relationship involves actors of different kinds—sultans and kings, rabbis and marabouts, merchants and peasants, ministries and defense firms—whose interactions unfold at different speeds. Third, the model allows legitimacy to be disaggregated. A diplomatic act may be popular for one reason (it affirms a long coexistence) and unpopular for another (it appears to condone the occupation of Palestinian land), and only a layered analysis can register this ambivalence.
Three clarifications are necessary at the outset. The first concerns the figure of two and a half thousand years. It is best read as a shorthand for deep antiquity rather than as an exact chronology. The earliest secure evidence of Jewish life in Morocco is epigraphic and archaeological and belongs to the Roman centuries, while the older traditions linking Jewish settlers to Phoenician navigation and to the aftermath of the destruction of the First Temple are plausible but poorly documented (Gottreich, 2020; Hirschberg, 1974). The adjective “unbroken” also requires qualification. Jewish presence in Morocco has been continuous, though its demography collapsed after 1948; but the relationship in the sense of state-to-state diplomacy has been intermittent, covert for long periods, and formalized only in 1994, in 2020, and in 2026 (Black & Morris, 1991; Shlaim, 2000).
The second clarification concerns terminology. For most of its history the relationship was one between Morocco and its own Jewish subjects, and between Morocco and the wider Jewish and Sephardic world, not between Morocco and a Jewish state. The State of Israel dates from 1948, and its relationship to Moroccan Jews has been complex: Israel became the destination of the majority of Moroccan Jewish emigrants, and Israelis of Moroccan descent are now among the largest components of its Mizrahi population, but they migrated into a society that frequently devalued their culture (Laskier, 1994; Shenhav, 2006; Shohat, 1999). The essay therefore distinguishes consistently among Moroccan Jews, Israeli citizens of Moroccan origin, and the Israeli state. To conflate these categories is both analytically careless and politically hazardous, because it invites the identification of Moroccan Jewish citizens with the policies of a government in which they have no part.
The third clarification concerns the verb “regulate.” The framing under discussion holds that the tiers regulate the relationship. In the sense used here, regulation means that each tier sets limits and provides resources to the others: the lower tiers legitimate and constrain the upper ones, and the upper ones in turn finance and protect the lower ones through state patronage of Jewish heritage, funding for synagogues and cemeteries, and the diplomatic cover that allows diaspora communities to visit and invest (Boum, 2013; Chtatou, 2023c). articles.title: Vision 2030: Saudi Arabia ten years on - www.thebusinesssoiree.com
articles.summary: Vision 2030: Saudi Arabia ten years on  www.thebusinesssoiree.com
articles.full_text:
When His Royal Highness Mohammed bin Salman, Crown Prince of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, unveiled the Vision 2030 plan in 2016, to the average European it sounded almost like an attempt to reinvent Saudi Arabia. In just fourteen years, a country dependent on oil was to transform itself into a modern economy open to tourists, foreign investors and new technologies.
Ten years have passed and four remain until the target date. How far have the Saudis actually come? The answer is not clear-cut. What can certainly be said, however, is that Vision 2030 has not remained merely a collection of grandiose fantasies and promises.
Saudi Arabia in 2026 is indeed, in many respects, a different country from the one it was it was ten years ago. This can be seen, for example, in the labour market. According to the official Vision 2030 – Annual Report 2025, unemployment among Saudis, which stood at 12.3 per cent at the start of the programme, has fallen to 7.2 per cent. And since the original target of seven per cent had already been achieved earlier, it was tightened in 2024 to five per cent by the end of the decade. The Kingdom is also close to its targets in other areas. The home ownership rate among Saudi households stands at 66 per cent, compared with a baseline of 47 per cent, while the target is 70 per cent. According to the latest available data, average life expectancy has risen to 79.7 years, practically matching the target of 80 years. Healthcare services are accessible to 97.5 per cent of the country’s population centres. Services, logistics, technology, tourism and other new sectors are also developing significantly, while the private sector’s share of GDP has risen from a baseline of 44 to 51 per cent. The target for 2030 is 65 per cent.
The most important question surrounding Vision 2030, however, is different – has Saudi Arabia managed to free itself from its dependence on oil? The answer is: partly. Non-oil activities accounted for approximately 55 per cent of real GDP in 2025. Oil therefore remains crucial to the Kingdom. According to current data from the International Monetary Fund, oil and petroleum products account for roughly 69 per cent of Saudi exports. Non-oil exports were equivalent to 22 per cent of non-oil GDP, while Vision 2030 aims for 50 per cent. Foreign direct investment stood at 2.8 per cent of GDP, compared with a target of 5.7 per cent. The Saudi economy is therefore much more diversified than it was ten years ago, but it has not yet broken its financial dependence on oil.
Design for one section of The Line.
One of the visible successes is tourism. In 2025, Saudi Arabia recorded approximately 123 million tourists, including 29.3 million from abroad and 93.3 million domestic tourists. The original target of 100 million was exceeded, so the Kingdom raised its target for 2030 to 150 million. Religious tourism plays a distinct role. The number of pilgrims arriving from abroad for Umrah, the lesser pilgrimage to Mecca, has risen from approximately six million a year to eighteen million. The target for 2030 is thirty million. Billions in investment in Red Sea resorts, culture, entertainment and sport are part of the same strategy. Formula 1, top-level football, boxing and golf are not merely a matter of prestige. They are intended to attract visitors and capital and help build new sectors of the economy.
Pilgrims at the Grand Mosque in Makkah.
The gigantic NEOM project, and above all the futuristic city of The Line, planned in its final form as a 170-kilometre-long strip of development, has attracted the greatest attention worldwide. But it is precisely here that extraordinary ambitions are colliding with economic reality. Some contracts have been suspended or terminated, and the original vision of rapidly building The Line has receded. For example, in May this year, the Italian company Webuild announced that NEOM had terminated its contract for a high-speed rail connection that had previously been suspended. This does not mean, however, that the entire project is dead, as work on other parts of NEOM is continuing. One example is the industrial development of Oxagon, where new projects are being prepared, including a large-scale data centre whose first phase is expected to require an investment of five billion dollars and, according to the plan, become operational in 2028. By contrast, although the island resort of Sindalah was officially opened as early as 2024, regular operations have yet to begin. This year, the project was taken over by developer Red Sea Global, which is expected to complete it and make it operational. Questions also remain over the timetable for the Trojena mountain resort, which was due to host the 2029 Asian Winter Games. However, the event was postponed this year and was ultimately awarded to Almaty, Kazakhstan.
Yacht marina within The Line.
Saudi Arabia has therefore not yet reached the finish line, but in many areas it is not far from it, and some targets have already been achieved. In its report from July this year, the International Monetary Fund unequivocally points to significant progress under Vision 2030, which has strengthened the non-oil economy, expanded the role of the private sector and brought measurable changes to the labour market. At the same time, it points out that reforms must continue, particularly in diversification, the business environment, education and support for small and medium-sized enterprises.
WOMEN AS A SYMBOL
One of the most striking indicators of Saudi Arabia’s transformation is the position of women in the labour market. When Vision 2030 was announced, their labour force participation stood at 22.8 per cent, with a target of 30 per cent for 2030. However, this was exceeded ahead of schedule, with the participation rate of Saudi women reaching 35 per cent in 2025, so the government raised the target by another ten percentage points. The number of women in leadership positions in companies and institutions has also increased significantly – according to the Ministry of Human Resources, women accounted for 43.7 per cent of middle and senior management positions in the second quarter of 2025. The changes have also been supported by labour law reforms, including strengthening the principle of equal treatment and prohibiting discrimination.

In a strategic shift, Saudi Arabia withdraws NEOM and four stadiums from its 2034 FIFA World Cup bid amid financial pressures.
According to a report by Semafor, five of the 15 stadiums that were intended to be built to host the FIFA World Cup 2034 are being reconsidered by Saudi Arabia. Due to higher costs and a change in funding priorities, the Saudi government, along with the Public Investment Fund (PIF), is revising its sports business plans regarding infrastructure. This reduction in scope is part of an overall change in plans related to the enormous development projects of the Kingdom that are in line with Vision 2030.
Planned Venues Reduced as Saudi Arabia Changes Focus of World Cup 2034
To deal with increased budgets, the PIF is considering cancelling five proposed stadiums in the bid for the 2034 World Cup. The cancelled stadiums include King Abdullah Economic City and Qiddiya Coast, located near Jeddah, along with Roshn and New Murabba in Riyadh. Moreover, the planned NEOM Stadium, which was to be constructed in ‘The Line’, is being cancelled as per a Reuters report, owing to a total halt in the project.
The Kingdom will now focus only on priority projects, including the King Salman International Stadium and Prince Mohammed Bin Salman Stadium in Riyadh. Six new stadiums and four refurbished stadiums will be included in the Kingdom’s tournament map. Four stadiums will be tested when they host matches for the AFC Asian Cup in 2027.
Financial Pressure and Regional Instability Shift Saudi Arabia’s Priorities
The decision to reduce the number of World Cup venues is consistent with Saudi's strategy of pulling back its huge investments in sports and infrastructure. With a tightening fiscal environment, the Kingdom has pulled back financing for the LIV Golf league and cancelled plans to host the 2029 Asian Winter Games at NEOM’s Trojena resort complex. Adding to these economic concerns is the issue of security.
Furthermore, the current situation of war and heightened tension has resulted in the prioritisation of security and stability for Saudi Arabia. In the end, the economic and security issues have made Saudi Arabia take a very conservative approach to their global aspirations.

- Last week saw 10 attacks on commercial vessels in and near the Strait of Hormuz, according to the U.K. navy, which said October has become the worst month for attacks on shipping in the strait since the early days of the war in March. Crude oil prices remain over $105 a barrel after hitting a five-month high near $110 over the weekend.
Russia's foreign minister condemns U.S.-Iran attacks on Iran in first visit to Tehran since war began
Iran's top security official called for stronger cooperation with Russia to bolster regional security after meeting with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov in Tehran on Monday, Iran's state-run IRNA news agency said.
Gen. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, said that cooperation could include joint economic projects, such as the completion of transportation corridors. Lavrov, meanwhile, condemned the U.S.-Israeli military attacks on Iran as illegal during his first visit to Iran since the U.S. launched its war with Iran almost eight months ago.
Also in Tehran on Monday, Iran summoned Germany's ambassador over what it called baseless accusations, the Iranian Foreign Ministry said. Germany had summoned Iran's ambassador in Berlin the same day after a court sentenced two men with ties to Iran's intelligence service for plotting to kill the leader of a Jewish organization in Germany.
President Masoud Pezeshkian also said Iran is willing to resolve tensions through dialogue, blaming U.S. interference for divisions in the region, state-run IRNA reported.
Pezeshkian made the remarks during Monday's meeting with Lavrov, saying the presence of U.S. military bases in neighboring countries had only increased tensions, instability and insecurity.
Netanyahu tells Trump "we have a job to finish" on Iran
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu released a video on Monday of a phone call between him and President Trump, in which the two leaders traded praises and suggested they may again attack Iran together.
Netanyahu shared the call one day after Mr. Trump endorsed his reelection bid. In it, the U.S. president could be heard telling the prime minister on speakerphone: "I think you're going to have a tremendous victory, actually."
"You're the man I want by my side, Bibi," Mr. Trump said, referring to Netanyahu by his nickname.
Netanyahu hailed Mr. Trump for joining Israel in attacking Iran in late February.
"Donald, we have a job to finish," a beaming Netanyahu said. "We'll finish it together. We'll finish it, and no one else will do it."
Netanyahu did not elaborate but again described Iran's clerical state, which remains in power nearly eight months after the joint attack, as "the greatest danger."
CBS/AFP
Houthis claim to have carried out 6 military operations in Saudi Arabia in 48 hours
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said in a statement Monday that the group had carried out six military operations in Saudi Arabia over the previous 48 hours, amid a sharp escalation in hostilities between the Iran-backed group and the kingdom.
Saree said the attacks targeted military sites, airports and oil infrastructure, including King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Aramco facilities in Yanbu on the Red Sea coast, and the Shaybah oil field near the border with the United Arab Emirates.
Other strikes hit Abha International Airport, radar installations, Khamis Mushait air base in southwestern Saudi Arabia, a Saudi naval force camp, and a separate radar site in Bir Askar in the kingdom's south, according to Saree.
He described the attacks as retaliation for more than 200 Saudi strikes and missile attacks on Houthi-held areas over the previous 48 hours, saying the Houthis would pursue a policy of "escalation for escalation" until attacks on Yemen cease.
On Sunday, the Houthi-run Health Ministry blamed Saudi-led forces for airstrikes that killed or wounded more than 30 people in Yemen's rebel-held territory over the weekend, including one in the northern province of Saada that left at least nine dead. Five children and two women were among those killed, according to the rebel group.
AP/AFP
At least 53 killed in Houthi strike on Yemen's government forces
At least 53 soldiers were killed and another 200 recruits were injured at a military camp on Monday, when Houthi rebels struck Yemeni forces with ballistic missiles, Yemeni military officials said. The targeted camp is in the southern province of Shabwa. The provincial government there also acknowledged the strike, as did the Iran-backed rebel group.
The attack was one of the deadliest since fighting resurged between the Houthis and Yemen's Saudi-backed government forces this summer, as a widening front in the Iran war that began in February.
The provincial government in Shabwa said the death toll from Monday's attack could rise.
"This bloody, treacherous attack targeted new recruits in the training and preparation phase and is considered an extremely critical military escalation and a blatant aggression on the security and stability of Shabwa province," the provincial government said in a statement, which also called on Yemen's president, the Saudi-led coalition and the government to expedite air defense and early warning systems to reinforce Shabwa's capabilities.
The head of Yemen's ruling Presidential Leadership Council, Rashad al-Alimi, promised a "firm response" and said the attack reflects the Houthis' "approach of resorting to cowardly terrorist attacks whenever they face pressures or their Iranian-backed sabotage plots falter."
One Yemeni military official said the missiles struck while recruits were lining up in formation for a training session. The official spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to talk to the media.
CBS/AP
Riyadh residents receive alerts warning of "hostile aerial threat"
Residents of Riyadh, Saudi Arabia's capital city, received alert messages from authorities on Monday that warned of "a hostile aerial threat." AFP journalists received the alerts, too, which were sent to their phones, according to the outlet.
"A warning has been issued by the National Early Warning Platform in Riyadh City to alert of a potential danger," Saudi Arabia's civil defense agency said in a statement on X. The agency also reported that the same warning had been issued for the nearby Kharj area.
A woman in her thirties living in northern Riyadh said she heard the sound of explosions, telling AFP: "we got used to this."
The warning, which often signals incoming Houthi attacks, was lifted shortly after the defense agency's announcement. But it came as attacks by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis have intensified in Saudi Arabia. Hours later, the Houthis claimed a series of missile and drone attacks on Riyadh's international airport and other targets across the kingdom over the past two days.
CBS/AFP
Saudi investment conference will be pushed to 2027, its CEO confirms
A major Saudi investment conference has been postponed to next year, its chief executive officer said on Monday, as the kingdom comes under repeated attacks from Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis.
Maha Al Saud, the CEO of the annual Future Investment Initiative (FII) Institute, said the event, which was scheduled to take place in Riyadh from Oct. 26 to 29, would instead happen in 2027 in a statement posted on X. She said organizers wanted to ensure the gathering's tenth anniversary edition delivered the "full scale" and "extraordinary quality" participants expected.
"This decision comes from a deep commitment to our partners, members, speakers and delegates," her statement said, adding: "A decade of partnership and shared vision deserves nothing less than our absolute best."
New conference dates will be announced soon, while current registrations and partnerships will remain valid, according to the statement.
For nearly a decade, the conference has served as a showcase for Saudi Arabia's efforts to attract global investors, business leaders and heads of state. The postponement dealt a blow to the kingdom's ambitions to draw foreign capital, diversify its oil-reliant economy and push its reform agenda.
Three sources familiar with the matter had earlier told AFP the conference would be postponed.
CBS/AFP
Egyptian parliament postpones debate on military support to Saudi, state media reports
Egypt's parliament on Monday postponed its debate on President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi's request to authorize military support to Saudi Arabia, which has faced mounting attacks from Yemen's Houthis, Egyptian state media reported. The debate has been delayed until next week, according to the report.
"House Speaker Hisham Badawi has adjourned the second parliamentary session dedicated to discussing authorization for taking necessary measures to support and assist the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, with discussions set to resume on October 26," Egypt's state-run Al-Akhbar newspaper reported.
The postponement concluded a second day of parliamentary sessions in which Egyptian lawmakers weighed Sisi's request to approve support for Saudi Arabia, if requested by the kingdom. An emergency session on Sunday also ended without a decision.

CAIRO (AP) — Iran-backed Houthi rebels struck Yemeni government forces with ballistic missiles on Monday, killing at least 53 soldiers at a military camp in one of the deadliest attacks since a resurgence in fighting this summer, Yemeni military officials said.
The attack wounded an additional 200 recruits at the military camp in the southern province of Shabwa, the provincial government there said. The rebels acknowledged targeting the camp.
The fighting between the Houthis and Yemen’s Saudi-backed government forces is a widening front in the Iran war that began in February. The escalation shattered a 2022 ceasefire deal that largely stopped fighting in Yemen’s civil war.
The Houthis have put their growing military capabilities on display on multiple fronts in recent weeks, repeatedly striking Saudi Arabia’s main international airport hundreds of miles (kilometers) away and seizing territory inside Yemen near a key shipping chokepoint.
In a sign that the Houthi attacks are unsettling Saudi society, the kingdom on Monday canceled a global investment conference scheduled for next week and extended an order for schools in and around Riyadh, the capital, to teach students remotely.
AP correspondent Charles de Ledesma reports Houthi rebels have hit a government location in southern Yemen, killing at least 53 people.
Iran and its allies in Lebanon and Iraq provide expertise, training and sophisticated weapons to the Houthis, according to U.N. and other experts. Iran denies arming the Houthis, which would violate a U.N. embargo.
The provincial government in Yemen says death toll may rise
The provincial government in Shabwa said the death toll could rise from Monday’s attack, which it said “targeted new recruits in the training and preparation phase and is considered an extremely critical military escalation.”
It called on Yemen’s president, the Saudi-led coalition and the government to expedite air defense and early warning systems to reinforce Shabwa’s capabilities.
The head of Yemen’s ruling Presidential Leadership Council, Rashad al-Alimi, promised a “firm response.”
A Houthi military spokesman claimed the camp was targeted because it is operated by Saudi officers, and that some of them were killed in the attack — though he provided no evidence. The Saudi government did not immediately comment.
A group of fighters aligned with the government said Monday its fighters repelled a Houthi offensive after hours of fighting in southwestern Yemen. Separately, the local authorities in Yemen’s Marib province said the Houthis fired ballistic missiles at the densely populated city of Marib, which hosts large numbers of people displaced by the conflict.
Separately, the Houthi-run Health Ministry said a father and his daughter were killed Monday when a mortar shell hit homes in the Sabir al-Mawadim district of Yemen’s Taiz province.
Saudi Arabia cancels investment conference
On Sunday, the Houthi-run Health Ministry blamed Saudi-led forces for an airstrike that killed at least nine people in Yemen’s rebel-held northern province of Saada. Five children and two women were killed in the attack, one of several that killed or wounded more than 30 people over the weekend, according to the rebels.
There was no immediate comment from Saudi Arabia.
The Houthis, a Shiite religious and political movement rooted in northern Yemen, are increasingly attacking Saudi Arabia because it supports Yemen’s internationally recognized government in the civil war.
The Sunni kingdom, which has long feared the emergence of a well-armed ally of Shiite Iran on its border, joined the war in 2015 after the rebels seized much of northern Yemen, including the capital, Sana’a.
In recent weeks, the Houthis have targeted Saudi airports, oil and military facilities, and the headquarters of Saudi oil giant Aramco.
On Monday, Houthi rebels claimed to have carried out six attacks targeting oil infrastructure, airports and military sites across Saudi Arabia, but the group did not specify when the attacks took place.
The Saudi Civil Defense issued danger alerts but no immediate reports of casualties or damage.
In Yemen, the Houthis recently seized more territory along the Red Sea coast and near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a crucial shipping alternative to the Strait of Hormuz. The Saudi-led coalition launched a major military offensive earlier this month to dislodge the rebels from that strategic perch and retake the territory.
Monday marked five years since Houthis detained more than 20 Yemeni staff of the U.S. embassy in Sana’a. The embassy had suspended operations in 2015 but local staff still provided security and basic maintenance of the facility. The State Department on Monday called for their “immediate and unconditional release.”
___
Associated Press writers Ahmed al-Haj in Aden, Yemen, and Baraa Anwer in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, contributed to this report.

U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is in the Middle East.
Meanwhile, Israeli police have arrested 10 suspects in a wave of settler violence that targeted a U.S. journalist and European diplomats in the occupied West Bank, and Iran-backed Houthi rebels announced attacks in Yemen and across Saudi Arabia.
Here’s the latest news from the Middle East on Monday. Read our full coverage here.
Hegseth makes surprise trip to Middle East
U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has made an unannounced trip to the Middle East.
Hegseth announced on social media late Monday U.S. time that he was in the Middle East visiting troops that were on an unspecified, “historic mission.” However, the post also came several hours after Axios reported that Hegseth was in Israel visiting Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
When asked about the visit and the reports, the Pentagon declined to comment.
Saudi Arabia executes 2 Bangladeshis over ‘indecent acts’
Saudi Arabia has executed a Bangladeshi man and woman after they were convicted of committing “indecent acts” in a mosque in the Muslim holy city of Mecca.
Bangladesh said that it wasn’t informed before the sentences were carried out and has sought information from Saudi Arabia. The Saudi Interior Ministry said the Bangladeshis were executed because of “the gravity and seriousness of their actions in violating the sanctity of both time and place.” It did not elaborate.
Israel arrests 10 suspects following settler violence
Police said 10 suspects were arrested on Monday following violent attacks by Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank that prompted heavy criticism of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government. Israeli police didn’t identify who attacked the people who had come to support Palestinians during their annual olive harvest.
Washington Post photographer Heidi Levine was beaten Friday by a crowd of young male settlers while documenting the scene, leaving her with several broken ribs and vertebrae. Masked settlers also attacked a group of European diplomats on Saturday. Palestinians have been subject to surging attacks, rarely leading to arrests or punishment, rights groups say.
Netanyahu’s main rival in the Oct. 27 elections, Gadi Eisenkot, said “a handful of criminals is burning up the last shreds of legitimacy left to the state of Israel.”

Skau said Monday in a video briefing that “life in Gaza remains absolutely brutal” and incredibly dangerous, with U.N. teams recording about 50 attacks per day in the past week, while in the West Bank, he saw burned olive fields, camps and villages. The Israeli military said it struck Hamas militants in each of the attacks on Gaza City. It did not comment on the other attack. Israel continues to launch deadly attacks on the enclave more than a year after Israel and Hamas struck a ceasefire deal.
