The United Kingdom’s top diplomat warned companies against violating international law by helping to build Israeli settlements in the West Bank. Their construction has surged under Netanyahu’s government, which views the West Bank as the Jewish homeland and opposes a Palestinian state.
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the E1 settlement project approved by Israel, which would cut the West Bank in two, “is a direct threat to the prospect of a two-state solution.” Israel’s top diplomat responded by saying his country wouldn’t be “intimidated by threats.”
Iran embraces Russia, rejects German accusation of attack on Jewish leader

Gen. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said that cooperation could include joint economic projects, such as the completion of transportation corridors. Lavrov, meanwhile, condemned the U.S.-Israeli military attacks on Iran as illegal.
Also in Tehran on Monday, Iran summoned Germany’s ambassador over what the Iranian Foreign Ministry called baseless accusations. Iran president says country has no ‘fundamental disagreements’ with neighbors

Pezeshkian said during Monday’s meeting with Lavrov that U.S. military bases in neighboring countries increased tensions, instability and insecurity.

Qatar-France Economic Partnership Expands Beyond Trade
Qatar and France are pursuing a deepening economic relationship that links capital with advanced industry and French technical expertise with emerging Qatari market opportunities, according to the Qatar News Agency. The agency reported that the partnership now spans trade, investment, corporate presence and strategic cooperation across several growth sectors.
Data from the National Planning Council showed that merchandise trade between the two countries reached approximately QAR 6.39 billion in 2025. That total comprised about QAR 2.44 billion in Qatari exports and QAR 3.95 billion in imports, leaving a trade deficit of roughly QAR 1.50 billion. Qatari exports included about QAR 1.51 billion of domestically produced goods and QAR 937.9 million in re-exports.
For 2026, the latest figures put bilateral trade at approximately QAR 1.32 billion, with Qatari exports valued at QAR 416.3 million and imports at QAR 904.9 million. The agency noted that the figures point to the importance of broadening Qatar's export base and strengthening the presence of locally produced goods in the French market.
Qatar has also committed to invest EUR 10 billion across key sectors of the French economy, including areas of mutual benefit, while more than 665 French companies operate in the Qatari market.
Priority Sectors for Cooperation
Energy, artificial intelligence, advanced technologies, infrastructure and financial services are identified as key growth sectors driving diversification amid global economic shifts. Banking expert Abdullah Al Raisi told the agency that the ties rest on a strong foundation for moving toward a more advanced phase of trade and investment cooperation, supported by mutual interests and opportunities in value-added industries that align with Qatar National Vision 2030.
Al Raisi said the trade figures demonstrate the strength of the partnership and the significance of the French market for Qatari companies. He identified advanced technology, artificial intelligence, clean energy, digital transformation, financial services and tourism as high-potential areas, and pointed to scope for drawing on French expertise in infrastructure and strategic projects in Qatar.
He added that strengthening the partnership should extend beyond raising trade volumes to attracting high-quality investment, establishing joint ventures, facilitating knowledge and technology transfer, and widening private sector participation in both countries.
Long-Term Partnership and Energy Links
Economist Dr. Abdullah Al Khater told the agency that the Qatari-French partnership is long-term, diverse and robust, citing the presence of more than 665 French firms in Qatar across sectors ranging from energy, led by TotalEnergies, to large-scale infrastructure.
On Qatari investment in France, Al Khater noted Qatar's role in French energy security through liquefied natural gas deliveries to the Fos Cavaou terminal in southern France. He also cited a memorandum of understanding between the Qatar Financial Centre and the French Chamber of Commerce that eases market entry for French firms expanding in Doha, in support of Qatar National Vision 2030.
The agency reported that the French presence in energy and infrastructure complements the investment opportunities Qatar offers, while the French market gives Qatari investors access to strategic sectors and portfolio diversification. It added that French companies in Qatar open the way for partnerships that go beyond project execution to supply chain development, expertise transfer, stronger local capabilities and greater participation by Qatari companies in projects with an international dimension.
Energy remains central to the relationship, with continued collaboration between Qatar and French firms in the sector and a role for liquefied natural gas in supply security and energy source diversification. Advanced technology, artificial intelligence, digital transformation and sophisticated industrial sectors are also cited as areas for deeper cooperation.
Cooperation among financial institutions, chambers of commerce and business communities is described as another route to expanding ties by supporting business growth, facilitating market entry, encouraging communication between investors and exploring joint ventures.
The agency concluded that trade, investment volumes and corporate presence together indicate a partnership with a broad base for growth and room for greater integration. It identified enhancing Qatari exports to France, attracting high-quality investment, expanding joint ventures and linking commercial cooperation with knowledge and technology transfer as paths to higher economic returns, with shared objectives centered on a more diverse and sustainable partnership.

articles.full_text:
Qatar is preparing to announce a new regional defense partnership as threats to Gulf security intensify, with the country's deputy prime minister warning Monday that the economic fallout from disruptions to regional energy supplies has yet to reach its peak.
Speaking at the Global Security Forum in Doha, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of State for Defense Affairs Sheikh Saoud bin Abdulrahman al-Thani said Qatar was working with regional partners on new defense initiatives, according to Al Jazeera.
"I'm happy to say that soon we're going to announce a new partnership," Sheikh Saoudsaid.
He did not identify the countries expected to participate in the initiative or specify when it would be announced.
Sheikh Saoudsaid Qatar had recently reviewed its defense capabilities and identified air defense, counter-drone systems, cybersecurity and water security as key priorities.
He also emphasized the importance of cooperation among Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) member states while acknowledging their differing foreign policies.
"The main thing is we agree on the fundamental together," he said, adding that "every country has its own foreign policy."
Sheikh Saoudwarned that the economic repercussions of disruptions to Gulf energy supplies could become more severe in the coming months.
"We haven't reached the peak with respect to energy," he said, warning of further consequences "in the coming days and months."
He identified threats to national sovereignty, disruptions to energy supplies and the spillover of regional conflicts as major challenges facing Qatar and neighboring Gulf states.
His remarks came months after Iranian attacks in March damaged Qatar's Ras Laffan industrial complex, one of the world's major liquefied natural gas (LNG) production hubs.
Sheikh Saoudstressed that instability in the Gulf could have consequences far beyond the region because of its central role in international energy markets and trade.
He warned that disruptions could affect the "chain of supply from east to west and also from west to east."
The deputy prime minister added that worsening regional insecurity could also affect Gulf investments in Europe and the United States, as well as financial assistance provided by Gulf countries to other nations.
Sheikh Saoudcredited cooperation with the United States for strengthening the Gulf's defensive capabilities.
He said decades of military investment, shared expertise and coordination had improved the ability of regional countries to intercept incoming threats.
According to Sheikh Saoud, "more than 90 percent of attacks" during the conflict had been prevented through those capabilities.
He presented the figure as evidence of the importance of sustained defense cooperation between Gulf countries and Washington.
The planned regional partnership would come as Qatar seeks to reinforce its military preparedness against missile and drone threats while addressing vulnerabilities in critical infrastructure.
The remarks followed a meeting Thursday between Syrian Interior Minister Anas Khattab and his Qatari counterpart, Khalifa bin Hamad bin Khalifa Al Thani, in Damascus.
Khattab received the Qatari minister, who also heads Qatar's Internal Security Force, known as Lekhwiya, and his accompanying delegation at Tishreen Palace, according to Syria's Interior Ministry.
The meeting addressed "a number of issues and matters of mutual interest" and ways to "strengthen security cooperation and coordination between the two interior ministries in a manner that serves the interests of both countries and peoples and supports the foundations of security and stability," the ministry said.
The discussions reflected continuing efforts by Doha and Damascus to expand bilateral security cooperation.
The two interior ministers previously discussed security cooperation during a meeting in Doha on Sept. 4, 2025, according to the Qatar News Agency (QNA).
Khattab said at the time that the talks addressed "ways to strengthen joint cooperation, particularly in security fields of mutual interest."
During his visit to Qatar, the Syrian minister toured the headquarters of Lekhwiya and the National Command Center, where he was briefed on crisis management technologies and operational systems.
The visit also included discussions on strengthening security and administrative cooperation and exchanging expertise.
The renewed engagement with Syria comes as Qatar pursues broader regional defense arrangements and seeks to strengthen security coordination amid growing threats to Gulf infrastructure, energy supplies and international trade.

articles.title: St. Petersburg oil site burns as 1,000 Ukrainian drones bite Russia
articles.summary: Ukrainian drone strikes set an oil export terminal ablaze in St. Petersburg Sunday as Kyiv launched more than 1,000 drones across Russia in one of its largest aerial bombardments t...
articles.full_text:
Ukrainian drone strikes set an oil export terminal ablaze in St. Petersburg Sunday as Kyiv launched more than 1,000 drones across Russia in one of its largest aerial bombardments to date.
The attack comes amid deepening tensions between Ukraine and Washington , with U.S. President Donald Trump criticizing Kyiv for its strikes on Russian oil infrastructure.
One person was killed and five more were wounded in the attack, which sparked fires at both the Petersburg Oil Terminal and the city’s Ruchi oil depot, said local Gov. Alexander Beglov.
A logistics center belonging to Russian retailer Ozon and a data center for local tech giant VK were also targeted, both companies confirmed.
Russia's Defense Ministry said Sunday that its forces had destroyed 1,015 Ukrainian drones over 15 Russian regions, as well as the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the Black Sea.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told Russian state news agnecy Tass that Kyiv was "resisting" Moscow's invasion, but that Ukraine could not "change the current course of events."
Meanwhile, a woman died and at least two other people were wounded, including a 6-year-old girl, after Russia launched two attacks on the southern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia, local officials said.
Two apartment buildings, 18 cars and an educational institution were damaged as a result of the attack, head of the Zaporizhzhia Regional Military Administration Mykhailo Semikin said.
U.S. President Donald Trump announced on Oct. 11 that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an "energy cease-fire" in the 4 1/2-year-old war, but offered no details on it and Kyiv reported attacks by Moscow on energy sites after his statement.
Ukraine confirmed Thursday it had resumed attacks on Russian oil after a three-day hiatus.
Zelenskyy was outraged by Russia's continuing aerial bombardment of his country's energy infrastructure in apparent defiance of Trump's demand Sunday for both sides to halt those attacks. The Ukrainian government initially said that it was heeding the cease-fire.
In a post on X Sunday, Zelenskyy said that in the week since Trump’s announcement of an energy cease-fire, Russia had attacked Ukraine’s energy, oil and gas sectors 76 times.
He also said that in the past night alone, energy facilities in four Ukrainian regions had been attacked and tens of thousands of families were still without power. He accused Russia of trying to cause a blackout.
"America should see that Russia is not taking any reciprocal steps in response to sanctions relief or agreements. On the contrary, they take every signal of an opportunity to make money as proof that their bet on war is paying off and they can keep fighting," he wrote.
Zelenskyy also stressed that the war was continuing due to Russia’s invasion – not because Ukraine was defending itself.
"It is Russia that must face pressure for peace to have a chance. Thank you to everyone who understands this and helps," he said.
Trump told reporters Saturday that they don’t know what his decision is yet regarding further sanctions on Russia, despite the executive order he signed Friday night waiving planned restrictions, citing a U.S. national interest.
"We’ll figure it out, and you’ll figure it out. But it’s a very good decision, and it’s going to be a decision that’s good for the country, and I think good for the world," Trump said at a fundraising dinner at his Florida estate.

articles.title: Gaza funeral bid farewell to 75 dead under rubble of Israel's war
articles.summary: Hundreds of Palestinians attended a funeral Sunday for 75 people, including women and children, whose remains were recently recovered from beneath the rubble of Gaza City homes des...
articles.full_text:
Hundreds of Palestinians attended a funeral Sunday for 75 people, including women and children, whose remains were recently recovered from beneath the rubble of Gaza City homes destroyed by Israel during the early months of its genocidal war.
The funeral procession began outside the Daraj Sports Club before the remains were buried at Sheikh Radwan Cemetery in Gaza City.
The remains, wrapped in Palestinian flags, had been laid out at the site Saturday evening to allow relatives to bid farewell.
Abdullah al-Majdalawi, director of public relations and media for Gaza’s Civil Defense, told Türkiye's Anadolu Agency (AA) that the remains had been recovered over recent weeks from several destroyed homes in the Daraj neighborhood in northeastern Gaza City.
He said the buildings were bombed while residents were inside during the early months of the war and that the victims belonged to around 20 Palestinian families, including people who had been displaced to the homes.
Majdalawi said efforts to recover bodies from beneath the rubble continue to face severe difficulties due to a lack of equipment and heavy machinery.
The recovery operations are part of the second phase of the Civil Defense’s project to retrieve the bodies of Palestinians trapped under rubble, launched on July 19.
Civil Defense spokesman Mahmoud Basal said at the time that the phase would involve searching 147 destroyed homes across Gaza City and the northern and central parts of the enclave, where an estimated 1,072 bodies were believed to be trapped.
The first phase, launched in November 2025, recovered 333 bodies and remains out of 559 people believed to be buried beneath 54 destroyed homes and buildings. Limited resources prevented teams from reaching around 226 others.
Basal told AA on Oct. 7 that more than 8,000 missing Palestinians were still believed to be under the rubble and warned that recovering them with currently available resources could take around eight years.
Under the first phase of a cease-fire agreement in effect in Gaza since Oct. 10, 2025, Israel was expected to allow heavy equipment and machinery into the enclave, but Palestinian authorities and factions have accused it of failing to meet that and other commitments.
More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed and over 175,000 injured since Israel launched its genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023, while around 90% of the enclave’s civilian infrastructure has been destroyed.

articles.title: Israeli settler terrorism risks West Bank explosion, official warns
articles.summary: A senior Palestinian official warned Monday that mounting attacks by Israeli settler terrorists and Israeli forces could ignite a wider confrontation in the occupied West Bank, urg...
articles.full_text:
A senior Palestinian official warned Monday that mounting attacks by Israeli settler terrorists and Israeli forces could ignite a wider confrontation in the occupied West Bank, urging peaceful resistance as international criticism grows over settler terrorism, illegal settlement expansion and restrictions on Palestinian farmland.
Jibril Rajoub, secretary-general of the central committee of the Palestinian Authority's ruling Fatah movement, criticized the Israeli government for overseeing violence against Palestinians amid intensifying attacks by illegal Israeli settlers.
"The terrorism carried out by the army and settlers, under the supervision of the Israeli government... is a prelude to a coming reaction and explosion," Rajoub told Agence France-Presse (AFP) in Cairo.
Despite the escalating violence, Rajoub called for nonviolent resistance to the Israeli occupation, describing peaceful struggle as a strategic choice for Palestinians.
"Bloodshed is no longer an acceptable option," he said, urging Palestinians to confront the occupation peacefully despite continued Israeli attacks.
His remarks came during meetings in Cairo involving Palestinian political movements, including Fatah and Hamas, aimed at addressing longstanding divisions and establishing a unified political leadership.
The talks followed Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas' decision to postpone elections originally scheduled to begin next month until September 2027.
Rajoub said the discussions focused on unified political representation under a single governing authority and one legitimate armed force.
Hamas has governed Gaza since 2007, when the Palestinian political divide deepened following its takeover of the territory.
Germany on Monday condemned attacks by illegal Israeli settlers targeting European diplomats and an American photojournalist in the occupied West Bank, joining calls for an investigation.
German Foreign Ministry spokesperson Kathrin Deschauer described the incidents as troubling and expressed solidarity with those targeted.
The attacks occurred over the weekend near Taybeh, east of Ramallah, where a European delegation was visiting Palestinian communities during the annual olive harvest.
The delegation included French and Belgian consuls, a Polish representative and Catholic Church officials.
Masked Israeli settler terrorists confronted members of the delegation, while a window of a Belgian consular vehicle was smashed.
Deschauer said Berlin supported European demands for an investigation into the attacks.
Britain also condemned the violence and warned companies and individuals against participating in construction projects linked to illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband urged businesses to avoid bidding for tenders connected to the E1 settlement project, warning that involvement could result in legal consequences and sanctions.
"We urge businesses and individuals not to proceed with bids for E1 construction tenders," Miliband said Monday.
He said the British government had introduced new powers allowing sanctions against individuals and companies involved in constructing illegal Israeli settlements.
Miliband also reaffirmed London's commitment to legislation banning imports from illegal Israeli settlements and targeting services that finance or facilitate their expansion.
"This U.K. Government will not accept the continued displacement of Palestinians and the unlawful occupation that persists," he said.
"We will not be bystanders in the destruction of the two-state solution," he added.
United Nations experts warned Monday that Palestinian farmers face increasing settler terrorism, destruction of agricultural land and restrictions on access to their olive groves as the annual harvest begins.
The experts said attacks by illegal Israeli settlers have intensified in recent years, threatening the livelihoods of thousands of Palestinian families who depend on olive cultivation.
During the 2025 olive harvest, 178 settler attacks linked to harvesting activities were documented across 88 Palestinian towns and villages, the highest number of affected communities since 2020.
More than 6,000 olive trees and saplings were vandalized during the season, nearly double the 2024 figure and the highest number recorded in six years.
The experts also expressed alarm over Israeli military orders issued in September 2026 authorizing the removal of vegetation from approximately 339,000 square meters (84 acres) of Palestinian agricultural land.
The orders affect olive groves in Jenin, Qabatiya and Beit Rima and could lead to the uprooting of trees cultivated by Palestinian families for generations.
According to the experts, Palestinian landowners have been given extremely limited time to remove vegetation or challenge the orders.
Israeli authorities have also increasingly denied farmers permits to access their land, while revised military regulations prohibit Palestinians from harvesting olives on areas Israel designates as state land, including plots cultivated for generations.
The U.N. experts emphasized that olive farming is central to Palestinian food security, economic survival and cultural heritage.
They called on Israel to protect Palestinian farmers from settler attacks, guarantee access to agricultural land and fulfill its obligations under international law.
The experts also urged the international community to increase pressure on Israel to halt settlement expansion, prevent further displacement and ensure accountability for violations of Palestinian rights.
Settler terrorism has intensified across the occupied West Bank, where Palestinians face repeated assaults, theft, property destruction and attacks on agricultural communities.
The violence has escalated ahead of Israel's Oct. 27 elections, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu seeking another mandate alongside far-right allies who support expanding illegal Israeli settlements.
More than 500,000 Israeli settlers live in illegal settlements across the occupied West Bank, alongside approximately 3 million Palestinians.
Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territory are illegal under international law.
Since October 2023, at least 1,125 Palestinians have been killed in the occupied West Bank, most by Israeli forces, according to an AFP tally based on Palestinian Health Ministry figures.
United Nations figures indicate that illegal Israeli settlers have killed at least 23 Palestinians during the same period.
Meanwhile, Israel's genocidal attacks in the Gaza Strip have killed at least 74,459 Palestinians since October 2023, according to Gaza health authorities, whose casualty figures are generally considered reliable by the United Nations.

articles.title: Vital goods shipments to Gaza set to resume as Israeli strikes continue
articles.summary: Israel said Monday it would gradually reopen a vital commercial supply route into the war-battered Gaza Strip after a dayslong suspension, even as fresh Israeli strikes killed at l...
articles.full_text:
Israel said Monday it would gradually reopen a vital commercial supply route into the war-battered Gaza Strip after a dayslong suspension, even as fresh Israeli strikes killed at least five Palestinians and the blockaded enclave's population continued to struggle with severe shortages of essential goods.
COGAT, the Israeli military agency overseeing humanitarian affairs in Gaza, said the decision followed reports from merchants that Hamas authorities had withdrawn demands for payments of 10,000 shekels ($3,225) per truck.
The agency acknowledged that the merchants' accounts had not been independently verified but said shipments would resume gradually, with priority given to food and other essential supplies ahead of winter.
Gaza's Government Media Office on Thursday rejected allegations that it imposes taxes or fees on commercial trucks entering the enclave, accusing Israel of using the claims to justify restrictions on goods and calling for the daily entry of 600 trucks.
Israeli authorities also announced tighter financial oversight, requiring payments to be made through documented bank transfers. Merchants found to have paid Hamas would be excluded from the commercial shipment system.
Hamas rejected the characterization of the payments as mandatory fees, saying the 10,000-shekel contributions were voluntary donations from financially better-off Palestinians to a national fund supporting vulnerable families in the war-ravaged territory.
The decision comes amid a deepening humanitarian crisis in Gaza, where much of the population remains dependent on aid after three years of genocidal Israeli attacks, repeated displacement and severe restrictions on the entry of food, medicine and other necessities.
Although a U.S.-brokered cease-fire reached in October 2025 halted the heaviest fighting, Israeli forces have continued carrying out deadly attacks across the besieged Palestinian territory.
Palestinian health officials said at least five Palestinians, including a 14-year-old boy, were killed Monday in separate Israeli strikes in Gaza City and Khan Younis.
The Israeli military did not immediately comment on the latest killings.
According to Gaza health authorities, approximately 1,500 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli fire since the October 2025 cease-fire. Israel says four of its soldiers have been killed by Palestinian resistance fighters in Gaza during the same period.
Despite the cease-fire, Palestinians continue to face deadly Israeli attacks, widespread destruction and severe humanitarian hardship, with access to food and other basic necessities remaining heavily dependent on Israeli-controlled supply routes.

articles.title: Lavrov lands in Iran as Moscow attempts to mediate in Mideast war
articles.summary: Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov arrived in Iran Monday for his first visit since the start of the Middle East war, as Moscow attempts to mediate, according to Russian media....
articles.full_text:
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov arrived in Iran Monday for his first visit since the start of the Middle East war, as Moscow attempts to mediate, according to Russian media.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said Sunday the trip would focus on "regional and international developments."
Lavrov will meet Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, according to the Russian Foreign Ministry.
Lavrov said Moscow's efforts "aim to prevent a return to large-scale war." Talks between Tehran and Washington have stalled.
His visit follows Russian President Vladimir Putin telling Pezeshkian in early October that Moscow was prepared to contribute to mediation efforts.
Russia and Iran, two of the world's most heavily sanctioned nations, maintain close ties. Their military and economic cooperation increased since Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine.
The Russian Foreign Ministry said discussions during Lavrov's visit would focus on "ways to resolve the acute international crisis triggered by the unlawful aggression of the U.S. and Israel against Iran."
The ministry said the war was a blow to stability and security "not only in the Near and Middle East, but also globally."
Despite a cease-fire in April and a U.S.-Iran memorandum of understanding in June, hostilities in and around the Strait of Hormuz continue.
In a separate development Monday, Iran's Revolutionary Guards said an oil tanker caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz after hitting a mine, the latest such incident since Tehran tightened its grip of the waterway.
"An oil tanker, which was in violation, struck a naval mine south of the Strait of Hormuz, resulting in an explosion and a fire in its engine room," Iranian state media quoted the Guards as saying.
The tanker was traveling in the strait's "unauthorized southern route" and had disabled its positioning and navigation systems, the statement said.
It came a day after the Guards said two oil tankers caught fire in the strait, both after hitting mines.
The Guards' naval commander Adm. Ali Ozmaei warned this week that any vessel that deactivated its navigation systems would be considered "hostile."
Iran claims control of the strategic waterway – through which one-fifth of the world's hydrocarbons pass in peacetime – and regularly targets vessels crossing without its authorization. In response, Washington maintains a naval counterblockade on Iranian ports.

articles.title: Israel nabs 10 over settler attacks on US journo, European diplomats
articles.summary: Israeli police arrested 10 suspects Monday in connection with weekend violence in the occupied West Bank, including separate attacks on a U.S. photojournalist and European diplomat...
articles.full_text:
Israeli police arrested 10 suspects Monday in connection with weekend violence in the occupied West Bank, including separate attacks on a U.S. photojournalist and European diplomats.
The United States, Israel's closest ally, had urged a crackdown on settler violence and the arrest of the perpetrators of the attack on the Washington Post photojournalist.
France, Belgium and Poland, whose diplomats were attacked, also called on Israel to take action.
Police said the suspects were arrested in a predawn operation on suspicion of involvement in acts of violence, violating a closed military zone order and illegal construction.
The suspects, whom police did not identify, were taken into custody for questioning. Israel's Army Radio reported that they were Israeli citizens.
Prosecutions of Israeli settlers, however, are rare.
U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee said on X that the arrests were "a very positive development in finding & punishing those who severely attacked and beat" Washington Post journalist Heidi Levine.
A video released by the police of the predawn operation appeared to show at least one arrested suspect, whose face is not seen, wearing ritual tassels known as tzitzit, which are often worn by religious Jewish men.
The video also appeared to show two slingshots, which can be used to hurl stones, being found at one property. On Friday, when the Washington Post journalist was attacked, dozens of masked settlers, some armed, descended on a Palestinian olive harvest, with some settlers hurling stones with slingshots.
Police, military forces and the Shin Bet domestic security service took part in the operation.
Referring to the West Bank by its biblical name, Judea and Samaria, Israeli Police Commissioner Daniel Levy said the law applied to everyone, "regardless of identity or affiliation."
"The Israel Police is committed to professional, equal, and impartial law enforcement, based on evidence and in accordance with the law," he said in a statement announcing the arrests.
Masked Israeli settlers were filmed Friday assaulting Levine, a U.S. citizen, who was covering a Palestinian olive harvest in the West Bank. Levine was taken to hospital and underwent surgery on a finger.
On Saturday, French, Belgian and Polish diplomats as well as a French mayor were attacked by masked settlers in another part of the West Bank. A Belgian diplomatic vehicle was also damaged.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar and the military have blamed "Israeli rioters" for the attack on the diplomats.
However, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whose far-right coalition is projected to lose its governing majority at the Oct. 27 election, has been more circumspect.
He has claimed the diplomats entered a "sensitive area with a history of confrontations" and without coordinating with the military. He has also said that the facts of the attack on Levine were "unclear."
Levine has said she was attacked by masked men wearing tzitzit tassels. Israel's President Isaac Herzog has apologized, saying the "violent rioters" who "brutally attacked" her did not represent the values of Israel.
Settler attacks on the Palestinians are surging, with at least 170 since Sept. 27, according to Yesh Din, an Israeli human rights group. Journalists, Israeli activists and foreign observers have also been targeted.

articles.title: Trump offers Netanyahu 'total endorsement' for Israeli election
articles.summary: President Donald Trump gave his "complete and total endorsement" to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu Sunday ahead of Israel’s Oct. 27 parliamentary election. "Bibi Netanya...
articles.full_text:
President Donald Trump gave his "complete and total endorsement" to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu Sunday ahead of Israel’s Oct. 27 parliamentary election.
"Bibi Netanyahu has been a Great Warrior Prime Minister, and an even greater Partner for Peace in combating the Islamic Republic of Iran," Trump wrote on Truth Social. Trump and Netanyahu launched their joint war against Iran in late February.
Trump claimed Iran had been destroyed militarily and financially. He threatened that if Tehran did not change course quickly, "we will soon finish the job."
"If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so," Trump wrote.
Trump said Netanyahu was "Strong, Brave, and Brilliant in the face of tremendous opposition, including from Israel itself," and was exactly the kind of partner the U.S. expected from Israel.
The statement clarified Trump's position, which had been unclear regarding his endorsement of Netanyahu's reelection bid.
Israeli public broadcaster Kan reported Trump said in a mid-June interview he would probably support Netanyahu in the election but needed to wait to see who would run. He added he had a good relationship with Netanyahu, but the Israeli prime minister needed to act more sensibly.
Following their intensified joint campaign against Iran, Trump and Netanyahu's interests appeared to diverge as the campaign continued, leading Trump to criticize Netanyahu publicly in unusually sharp terms.

articles.title: Alberta votes in referendum to seal fate of likely Canada secession
articles.summary: Residents of the oil-rich province of Alberta vote Monday in a referendum on whether to stay in Canada or start a process toward a legally binding secession vote. Recent polls show...
articles.full_text:
Residents of the oil-rich province of Alberta vote Monday in a referendum on whether to stay in Canada or start a process toward a legally binding secession vote.
Recent polls show about 70% of residents favor remaining part of Canada, while roughly 20% favor secession and the remainder are undecided.
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau and both of the country's major political parties have repeatedly opposed secession. Support for the independence movement has also come from former U.S. President Donald Trump.
Alberta, a province of about 5 million people, has about 3.1 million eligible voters, according to Elections Alberta, the province's election authority.
Polls open at 9 a.m. (3 p.m. GMT) and close at 6 p.m., though advance postal and in-person voting has already taken place.
Voters will decide 10 questions. The secession question will be counted first. Results could be available as early as Tuesday, according to election officials.
Calgary, with about 1.68 million residents, is Alberta's largest city, followed by the capital, Edmonton, with about 1.28 million. Its national parks in the Rocky Mountains attract tourists worldwide.
Alberta has some of Canada's most conservative voters. A movement advocating independence on cultural and economic grounds has existed for years.
Some oil industry representatives feel environmental regulations restrict them, while many protesters who opposed coronavirus restrictions and vaccine mandates later joined the independence movement.
Although the movement has long represented a minority of Albertans, it persuaded Smith, the province's conservative premier, to call the referendum. Smith herself has consistently advocated remaining part of Canada.

articles.title: Deaths reported when 'significant' blaze hits Canada military base
articles.summary: People were killed and injured in an incident that sparked a major fire at a military base in Alberta, Canada’s defense minister said Saturday, as reports indicated that large numb...
articles.full_text:
People were killed and injured in an incident that sparked a major fire at a military base in Alberta, Canada’s defense minister said Saturday, as reports indicated that large numbers of wounded were being taken to hospitals.
Fire crews scrambled late into the night as fierce winds whipped flames beyond Canadian Forces Base Wainwright and into the surrounding rural area.
It was not immediately clear how many people were killed or injured, but a doctor at a hospital in the city of Edmonton, 180 kilometers (120 miles) northwest, told Canada’s national broadcaster that patients were being brought to hospitals across the city as health-care facilities around the base became "completely overwhelmed" by the number of people needing care.
"This number of patients would overwhelm the city of Edmonton," Dr. Warren Thirsk, an emergency department physician at the Royal Alexandra Hospital, told CBC News. "It is more patients than any of us want to count right now. It’s a disaster. It’s a one in every 15- to 25-year disaster."
The town of Wainwright, near the base, has about 7,000 residents.
Defense Minister David McGuinty said the Royal Canadian Mounted Police were involved in investigating the incident and described the situation as "very, very active and delicate." He said authorities were still working to determine what happened and expected to provide further information.
The Royal Canadian Mounted Police said officers were called shortly after 4 p.m. Saturday following reports of a fire in a training area at the base.
Firefighters faced a volatile situation. Large areas of the province were hit during the day by a windstorm with gusts up to 100 kph (62.14 mph). The wind toppled some trees and sent signs flying and garbage cans rolling down streets.
By 11 p.m., the Municipal District of Wainwright said on social media the fire was being held and that property and critical infrastructure were protected. There was no evacuation order for residents.
McGuinty, speaking to reporters in Ottawa, confirmed the casualties but had no other details to share.
"I cannot recall such an incident in my short time for sure as a minister, but I cannot recall an incident like this in recent memory," McGuinty said.
"We will have more to say in the coming hours and days," he added.
He said Armed Forces members were at the scene and that RCMP were also involved. "This is an active and delicate situation and soon to be an active and delicate investigation."
Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe said his province was sending assistance to Alberta but did not specify what resources were being deployed.
"Our thoughts are with all the brave women and men affected," Prime Minister Mark Carney said earlier in a social media post.
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith described the fire as "significant and tragic" and said it was affecting many military personnel.
CFB Wainwright is one of Canada’s busiest military training bases, where soldiers prepare for combat operations. It is home to the Canadian Manoeuvre Training Centre, which conducts realistic battlefield exercises, and the 3rd Canadian Division Training Centre, which provides military training.
Canadian Conservative opposition leader Pierre Poilievre said he had spoken with Carney and the defense minister to offer support to those affected by the fire.
"Pray for Wainwright, everyone," Poilievre said in a social media post. He urged people in the area to follow emergency instructions and keep roads clear for first responders.
The fire also disrupted advance voting ahead of Monday’s referendum on whether Alberta should begin a process that could lead to independence from Canada.
Elections Alberta said two polling locations, in Lloydminster and Vermilion, closed early Saturday and the ballots were transported securely.

articles.title: Tourists trade cafes for barricades in France gripped by unrest
articles.summary: After travelling more than 20 hours by air from Australia, Anne Boland arrived to find the Louvre shut behind barricades, prompting her to offer a piece of advice to tourists plann...
articles.full_text:
After travelling more than 20 hours by air from Australia, Anne Boland arrived to find the Louvre shut behind barricades, prompting her to offer a piece of advice to tourists planning a trip to Paris.
"Stay home!" the 73-year-old pensioner told Agence France-Presse (AFP) on Monday outside the world's most visited museum, after a weekend of unrest that rocked some of the French capital's most iconic streets and squares.
She was one of thousands of visitors scrambling to navigate the City of Light as marches, traffic delays and wafting tear gas snarl the capital's 14-billion-euro ($16-billion) tourism industry.
A small group of protesters was blocking the entrance to the Louvre's famous glass pyramid, following days of mass protests that also spilled into some of the worst street violence France has seen in recent years.
Cycling through the city the day before, expecting charming Haussmann buildings, mansard roofs and corner cafes, Peter, a Dutch tourist, found himself touring a "war zone".
"It was terrible – debris from fires everywhere, glass on the pavement," the 63-year-old, who declined to give his last name, said.
Some shrugged off the disruptions. But almost all seemed caught off guard upon arriving at the Louvre, their plans suddenly cancelled.
Turned away, many resorted to selfies and photos in front of the former palace.
Roughly half a million people turned out across France on Saturday to denounce the surging cost of living, a culmination of earlier protests led by high school students demanding better conditions at their schools.
The Yellow Vests movement, which organized the weekend's rallies, has called for more protests this coming Saturday, as the government mulls partial, targeted curfews.
The closure of the Louvre meant just one more detour for Anne and her husband Pat Boland, also 73, whose airline lost their luggage during the voyage.
"It's just a disaster," said Pat with a laugh.
"We were here at this exact spot seven years ago, and the queues were too long," said Anne.
Having visited the museum twice, she's yet to go inside.
"We don't want to get involved. We want to stand back and get away from them," Pat said of the protests.
"But we don't want to go against them either," Anne hastened to add, noting a trend of cost-of-living protests cropping up across the world recently, including in Ireland and Australia.
At the weekend, taxi drivers at Charles de Gaulle airport warned arriving passengers that they might not be able to make it to their destination if protesters blocked their routes.
A headline in a newspaper in Wales, in the U.K., wondered if France would be safe for families to visit for the upcoming school holiday, and the U.S. embassy called on its nationals to exercise caution.
But many in the city carried on in typical Parisian style: a video broadcast by America's CBS news showed a couple drinking on a city terrace, unfazed by a nearby fire in the road.
"We haven't seen anything concerning," said Glenda Manna, 62, a university professor in town from the U.S.
But as the protests capture the attention of news channels – and politicians – around the world, there are incessant messages from family members back home pleading with them to "tell me you're safe," added her mother, Dorothy Hill, 82.

articles.title: Canada reveals military base fire fanned by high winds killed 4
articles.summary: A fire at a military base in Alberta killed four soldiers and injured dozens, Prime Minister Mark Carney said Sunday, calling it one of the worst peacetime tragedies for Canada's a...
articles.full_text:
A fire at a military base in Alberta killed four soldiers and injured dozens, Prime Minister Mark Carney said Sunday, calling it one of the worst peacetime tragedies for Canada's armed forces.
Carney announced the deaths without detailing the cause of the fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright Saturday.
"Four service members have lost their lives, and their loved ones have been notified," Carney said in Ottawa, noting that dozens more were seriously injured.
"This is one of the worst tragedies the Canadian Armed Forces have experienced on Canadian soil in peacetime," he said.
A doctor at a hospital in Edmonton, about 200 kilometers (110 miles) northwest of the base, told public broadcaster CBC that Wainwright's health care facilities were overwhelmed by patients.
"It is more patients than any of us want to count right now," Warren Thirsk said. "It's a disaster. It's a 15- to 25-year disaster."
The Department of National Defence said the fire broke out about 4 p.m. Saturday in the base's training area.
The Municipal District of Wainwright said on social media the fire spread rapidly because of high winds. It later said the blaze was contained, though firefighters would continue to monitor the area.
"Military and civilian crews fought this fire throughout the night in some of the worst conditions imaginable, risking their lives to protect their fellow Canadians," Carney said.
The base is one of the largest of the Canadian Armed Forces, regularly hosting training exercises with NATO personnel.
"We will care for the injured through every step of their recovery," Carney said. "And we will stand by the women and men of our armed forces as they bear the weight of this loss; they will not carry it alone because in Canada we take care of one another."
The fire disrupted advance voting for Monday's vote on starting the process toward a referendum on Alberta's independence.
Alberta's provincial elections office said the advance voting station in Wainwright closed.

articles.title: Kenyan starvation cult leader found guilty of killing 191 people
articles.summary: The leader of the Kenyan "starvation cult" Paul Mackenzie alongside 28 others were declared guilty of murder by a Mombasa ⁠court on Monday over the deaths of 190 children and an ⁠a...
articles.full_text:
The leader of the Kenyan "starvation cult" Paul Mackenzie alongside 28 others were declared guilty of murder by a Mombasa court on Monday over the deaths of 190 children and an adult in one of the world's worst cult-related tragedies in recent history.
The preacher was arrested in 2023 after police received a tip-off, and weeks later authorities began uncovering bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola Forest near the coast in southeastern Kenya.
Prosecutors say Mackenzie and his Good News International Church organized a Christian doomsday sect in which they ordered followers to starve themselves and their children to death to go to heaven before the world ended.
The case has gripped Kenya since the discovery of the mass graves.
It raised questions over how Mackenzie was able to continue to operate despite having been on the radar of the authorities since 2017, when his premises were searched by police.
In 2019, authorities shut down Mackenzie's church and he relocated to the Shakahola Forest, police said.
Mackenzie denied murder charges, saying he did not force the victims to starve, but the court rejected that argument.
He and the others convicted will be sentenced on Nov. 6. Defence lawyer Lawrence Obonyo, who represents Mackenzie and almost all of the others convicted, said he had been instructed to appeal.
Francis Wanje, 62, lost eight family members, including two grandchildren to the cult. He told Reuters that the judgment made him happy and gave him confidence in the judiciary.
"So many are going to learn from what has come up today. ... You find churches everywhere, but they've got ill reasons for the churches. So it is good for members of the public to be very careful," Wanje added.
In total, more than 400 bodies have been recovered from the Shakahola Forest.
Many of the children's bodies were severely decomposed, with only 26 able to be identified, and investigations into the other deaths are ongoing.
Justice Diana Kavedza Mochache said in a hearing lasting more than eight hours that, in some cases, children were isolated and denied food while their parents watched.
The director of public prosecutions, Renson Ingonga, told reporters afterwards at the Mombasa High Court: "That is the best judgment we would ever get."
Mackenzie was in court, wearing a striped polo shirt and red trousers, sitting alongside his wife, one of the co-accused.
When his name was read out by the judge he was silent, staring into space.
The case has led to calls for tougher oversight of churches and other religious organizations in a country where religious faith plays a prominent role in public life.
Kenyan President William Ruto said in 2023 that government agencies should have been able to prevent the deaths. He said he took responsibility as president.

articles.title: Iraq’s new Turkmen minister pledges co-op with Türkiye
articles.summary: In addition to Iraq’s Turkmen community, Mohammed Samaan Agha’s appointment as a state minister in Iraq was also welcomed in Türkiye. The minister, who also happens to be the leade...
articles.full_text:
In addition to Iraq’s Turkmen community, Mohammed Samaan Agha’s appointment as a state minister in Iraq was also welcomed in Türkiye.
The minister, who also happens to be the leader of the Iraqi Turkmen Front (ITC) and serves as governor of Kirkuk, promised to work “for the benefit of Iraq and Türkiye” in remarks to Turkish journalists on Sunday in Baghdad.
He met Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan on Saturday as the latter was in Baghdad to attend a meeting of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC).
Fidan congratulated him on his appointment as minister and told journalists that Türkiye had long monitored the challenges facing Iraq’s Turkmen community. He said addressing those challenges required progress on Iraq’s broader political and social problems.
”They are loyal citizens of Iraq. They are also highly conscious of preserving their own identity, which is precisely what we want,” Fidan said.
He stressed that the Turkmen community had consistently played a constructive role in Iraqi society and politics. “Türkiye and Iraq are brotherly countries, extensions of one another geographically, culturally and historically,” Fidan said. He called for a more institutionalized framework for bilateral cooperation that would serve both countries’ interests.
Agha was elected governor of Iraq’s Kirkuk province in April by the Kirkuk Provincial Council, becoming the first governor of Turkmen origin in more than a century. Turkmens are a Turkic-speaking minority whose total population is estimated at around 3 million. Agha visited Türkiye on an official trip following his election.
The new minister told reporters that, as a minister of Turkmen origin, he would work on issues in the interests of the people of both countries.
Commenting on his meeting with Fidan, Agha highlighted the historical, geographical, religious and cultural ties between the two countries.
Noting that Türkiye and Iraq shared many common issues, Saman Agha said: “We discussed all issues of mutual concern to the two countries, particularly security, trade, oil exports, energy, water and the fight against terrorism. In the coming period, as a Turkmen minister, we will do our best to carry out work in these areas that will benefit both countries and their peoples. We have initiated this process. God willing, we will make very good progress.”
Stating that regional tensions were negatively affecting the Iraqi economy, he said developments around the Strait of Hormuz and tensions between Iran, Israel and the United States had seriously harmed Iraq’s oil exports.
Emphasizing that Türkiye was an important neighbor and economic partner for Iraq, Agha said the Development Road Project should be accelerated.
“The faster the Development Road Project is carried out and implemented, the more beneficial it will be for Iraq. Türkiye will also benefit from it, but Iraq’s gains will be greater because this project will connect the East with the Western world,” he said.
Unveiled in May 2023, the Development Road Project is a $20 billion regional infrastructure initiative designed to facilitate the transport of goods from the Gulf to Europe via the Grand Faw Port in Basra, southern Iraq. The port would be linked to Türkiye and subsequently to Europe through an extensive network of railways and highways.
In April 2024, Türkiye, Iraq, the United Arab Emirates (UAE) and Qatar signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) on joint cooperation on the project.
Noting that the issue of water was becoming increasingly important as winter approached, Agha said water and security had also been discussed during talks between Türkiye and Iraq.
Recalling that Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi had also recently raised security concerns, the minister stressed the importance of strengthening cooperation between the two countries in these areas.
“I believe that relations between Iraq and Türkiye will become much stronger in the coming period,” he said.
Commenting on the Iraqi Turkmen Front’s political goals and the representation of Turkmens in the new government, Agha said they attached importance to maintaining good relations with the country’s different social groups.
“First and foremost, we trust in God. Then, we trust in the votes of our people and the support they have given us and the Iraqi Turkmen Front. At a very critical and difficult time for Iraq, we have established very good relations with our Shiite, Sunni and Kurdish brothers. We maintain sound and sincere relations with everyone,” the Turkmen minister said.
Recalling the agreement on rotating the governorship of Kirkuk among Turkmens, Kurds and Arabs, Agha said it was also significant that Turkmens had subsequently secured representation at the ministerial level in the government.
Emphasizing that all social groups in Iraq should be represented in the country’s administration, he said: “I think everyone in Iraq has now come to the conclusion that, alongside Shiites, Kurds and Sunnis, Turkmens and Christians must also be represented. This would allow all segments of Iraqi society to feel that they are represented in the government Cabinet.”

articles.title: Police arrest 1,800 after worst rioting in years shakes France
articles.summary: France grappled Sunday with widespread damage from violent protests that had led to 1,800 arrests, a torched historic town hall and looted shops. The unrest, which officials descri...
articles.full_text:
France grappled Sunday with widespread damage from violent protests that had led to 1,800 arrests, a torched historic town hall and looted shops.
The unrest, which officials described as extraordinarily intense, raised the stakes for President Emmanuel Macron. He is in his final months in power before elections in six months. The unrest followed weeks of student protests that also turned violent.
"About 1,800 people have been arrested, and investigations are underway to identify and prosecute perpetrators," Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said on X Sunday.
In Paris, where police said a record 855 people had been arrested, streets were littered with burnt-out barricades made of bikes, bins and other materials. Shop windows were smashed and cars torched on several streets.
The capital experienced "a level of violence that we have never, I believe, seen before," said Paris Deputy Mayor Lamia El Aaraje.
Masked youths pillaged scores of shops in Paris and many other cities, including Marseille, Bordeaux, Nice and Strasbourg, during the protests, which were called against high inflation and rising living costs.
Limoges' 19th-century town hall was destroyed by a fire that local prefect Maurice Barate told LCI television had been deliberately set by a "wild horde." Firefighters brought the blaze under control early Sunday.
Political recriminations followed the scenes of destruction.
Macron's centrist government and far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen both blamed "ultra-left" groups for the violence.
Far-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon, who had strongly backed the demonstrations, urged protesters late Saturday to avoid looting, describing it as "contrary to our methods."
Paris' Socialist Deputy Mayor Lamia El Aaraje accused Le Pen's party of fueling tensions related to the protests to further her ambition of becoming president next year.
The far-right National Rally party was "acting like a pyromaniac firefighter," El Aaraje said.
U.S. Vice President JD Vance also commented, implying that the unrest stemmed from immigration.
"Western liberals imported the third world into France and other countries in the name of diversity and compassion. They ignored fundamental questions of assimilation and compatibility," Vance said on X.
In Paris, where startled tourists ran with suitcases Saturday on streets filled with tear gas and protesters, the prosecutor's office said more than 500 people were in custody.
It said officials made arrests overnight into Sunday, with most held on suspicion of receiving stolen goods, association with intent to commit violence and vandalism.
Officials in Lyon said 160 people were in custody.
About 500 police officers, firefighters and paramedics were injured in the protests, Interior Minister Nunez said, adding the figure was provisional.
The violence occurred alongside nationwide cost-of-living protests, attended by 550,000 people according to the Interior Ministry, while the CGT union reported 800,000 participants.
Police used tear gas and water cannons against protesters who threw projectiles and aimed fireworks.
A crowd-control grenade blew off a 17-year-old boy's right hand in the southern city of Saint-Etienne.
Analyst Mujtaba Rahman of the Eurasia Group think tank said on X that Saturday's "terrible scenes were not political protest in any true sense. Most of the real demonstrations against high oil prices and failing schools were peaceful."
He added, "The violence came from a fringe of the ultra left. The looting by opportunistic gangs from the poor suburbs. All good news for Marine Le Pen."
During and after the demonstrations, gangs of youths roamed city streets, sporadically confronting police, setting fires and attacking shuttered stores to break in and empty shelves.
France's Yellow Vest movement, which staged protests eight years ago against planned fuel-tax hikes by Macron's government, called for Saturday's "yellow and youth" demonstrations.
The primary grievance was the cost of living, which the war in the Middle East partly drove up, contributing to soaring inflation in Europe and elsewhere.

U.S. President Donald Trump said Monday he would consider holding three-way talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, suggesting nuclear disarmament could be a central focus of the meeting.
"We would have it to talk about nuclear weapons and denuclearization," Trump told reporters outside the White House.
"If President Xi wants to have it, I'd have it."
Trump indicated that nuclear disarmament would be a priority in any such meeting.
"We would have it to talk about nuclear weapons and denuclearization," he said.
"We have more nuclear weapons than anybody. Russia is second, China is third, but catching up. China was way behind, and now they're catching up. It'll take about probably five years," Trump added.
Asked whether he would meet Putin and Xi to discuss ending the war without Zelenskyy present, Trump said he would do "anything I can do to end the war, whether somebody's there or not."
Earlier Monday, the Kremlin said that Putin, Trump and Xi could hold a three-way meeting on the sidelines of next month's APEC summit in China and that a potential meeting had come up in talks.
Trump also renewed his criticism of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, saying "it's time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine."
"Maybe it's time for Zelenskyy to get somebody else to negotiate," Trump told reporters.
"Zelenskyy doesn't know what he's talking about. Zelenskyy is a man that should have had this war settled a long time ago. If he would have listened to me, he would have made a much better deal a long time ago," Trump told reporters before departing the White House.
"I think it's time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine because what's happened? A tremendous number of people are dead. They're losing their male population," he said.
"Zelenskyy is not helping matters much. I think he doesn't want to stop it, but I want to see people not die."
"We've given a lot to Ukraine. They've given us nothing," he added.

articles.title: US seeks stronger Central Asia ties, greater business access
articles.summary: U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday that Washington aims to deepen its partnership with Central Asian nations as he pressed regional leaders to expand opportunities for...
articles.full_text:
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday that Washington aims to deepen its partnership with Central Asian nations as he pressed regional leaders to expand opportunities for American businesses.
Before heading to India on a tour mixing diplomacy and commerce, Rubio arrived in Uzbekistan's Silk Road city of Samarkand late Sunday for negotiations with top officials from Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and the Uzbek hosts.
The leaders of the five former Soviet republics met U.S. President Donald Trump at the White House in November last year, as the United States seeks stronger ties in a region with vast natural resources but where China has emerged as a key competitor.
Heading a delegation including numerous business executives, Rubio visited Samarkand's old city, a historic staging post between China and the West, before meeting regional leaders.
"The United States wants to be a strong partner in Central Asia, obviously rooted in this country, but also all the neighbouring countries who want to do more business and trade with us," he told journalists.
"We have an incredible delegation, almost 300 American businesses that are here with us, and the opportunity to sign billions of dollars of agreements that will both enrich the countries in the region, but also benefit the United States economically," he said.
Later Monday, the State Department said the U.S. and Uzbekistan had concluded more than 50 contracts worth a combined $12 billion in sectors including tech, industrial modernization, transport and energy.
With Washington stuck in a war with Iran and unable to halt Russia's invasion of Ukraine, Rubio has stepped up his foreign travel with recent trips to Europe and Latin America, while leaving Trump to handle the conflicts and the U.S. mid-term elections.
But Rubio insisted this week's tour is of strategic importance.
"This is an important relationship," he said shortly before his departure. "There's countries you'd like to get to because we want to build our relationships with them."
Asked by AFP whether Washington's push in Central Asia was aimed at countering China's growing influence, Rubio replied: "It's competition."
"There's no part of the world in which we feel like America and American business should not have a fair shot to compete."
Rubio also pushed back against suggestions there had been a "pause" in U.S .intelligence-sharing with Kyiv, and urged Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to "focus" on ending the war.
After Uzbekistan, Rubio will go to India, where the U.S. ambassador is Sergio Gor, who was born in Uzbekistan and is also the U.S. special envoy for Central Asia.
The Central Asian states remain linked to Russia by energy pipelines and security and migratory networks, but Russian influence has eroded since the start of its invasion of Ukraine.
And China has reaped the benefits. It is now the main trade partner of all five nations.
Chinese companies have signed a number of energy-related deals, seeking to buy natural gas in Turkmenistan, uranium in Kazakhstan and rare earths in Tajikistan.
In a joint statement after the talks, the U.S. and the five Central Asian countries pledged to "strive for a Central Asia that returns to the center of the global economy", including through development of the Trans-Caspian trade route.
Also known as the Middle Corridor, the route links China to Europe through Central Asia, the Caucasus and Turkey while bypassing Russia. It has attracted growing interest since Moscow's invasion of Ukraine.
Crossing Central Asia shortens delivery times while avoiding riskier routes, including the Red Sea-Suez Canal shipping corridor and overland routes through Russia, which have been complicated by Western sanctions.
On his second visit to India this year, Rubio will have stops in Mumbai and Jamnagar in Gujarat state. Both are major port cities.
"We're very close" to a trade deal with India, a second senior U.S. official said of negotiations with the Asian giant that have dragged on for months.
The two sides reached a provisional agreement in February aimed at reducing U.S. tariffs on Indian products.
But legal battles in U.S. courts over Trump's tariffs have fuelled uncertainty about when a bilateral trade deal could take effect.
India-U.S. relations were also rattled when Trump imposed 25% tariffs on Indian goods in retaliation for Delhi's purchases of Russian oil, but those duties have since been lifted.

articles.title: Heavy rain leaves at least 4 dead in eastern Spain
articles.summary: At least four people were killed and others were stranded on rooftops as heavy rain and floods battered Spain's Mediterranean coast, state broadcaster RTVE reported on Monday. Resc...
articles.full_text:
At least four people were killed and others were stranded on rooftops as heavy rain and floods battered Spain's Mediterranean coast, state broadcaster RTVE reported on Monday.
Rescue crews freed dozens of people who had been stranded since early morning, some on rooftops, in flooded buildings, or in vehicles.
Many roads, houses and campsites were underwater in the provinces of Valencia and Alicante. Floods also hit the Balearic Islands of Majorca and Ibiza.
Rescue operations used helicopters and boats, and even a surfboard: Police video showed a 93-year-old woman being brought to safety on one in Gandia.
The regional government declared the second-highest emergency level. Classes were suspended in more than 40 municipalities in the provinces of Valencia and Alicante.
Initially, authorities imposed a curfew of several hours for 145 municipalities with more than 800,000 residents in total.
By the afternoon, the curfew applied to only eight municipalities. However, several places remained cut off from the outside world due to the flooding.
The situation was particularly serious in the coastal town of Oliva, about 70 kilometres (43.5 miles) south of the provincial capital Valencia, where two bodies were recovered on Monday.
Storm system Adam had already caused chaos on the Spanish mainland at the weekend with extreme rainfall. Two people died: One woman in Sagunto in Valencia province, and another woman in Cabrera de Mar in Catalonia.
According to Mayor Yolanda Pastor, about 2,000 people were evacuated from seven campsites in Oliva.
"Many people are still trapped in their homes by the floodwaters," the mayor told the private broadcaster Antena 3. She said some people had climbed onto their roofs to escape.
A spokesperson for the emergency services said all people in life-threatening situations in Oliva had already been brought to safety.
Authorities in the hardest-hit areas in the south of Valencia province and the north of Alicante province urged people to stay in their homes where possible. The coastal regions of La Safor in Valencia and Marina Alta in Alicante were particularly affected.
According to Spain's state weather service AEMET, more than 530 millimetres of rain was recorded in Oliva within 24 hours. In the municipality of Pego in Alicante, just over 620 mm fell.
On Mallorca, the situation remained calm despite the highest red alert level declared for the night. Rescue services registered only three minor incidents: two fallen trees and a risk of collapse, which has since been resolved.
A total of 16 incidents were reported on the Balearic Islands, 11 of them on Ibiza and two on Formentera. Schools on all the islands had cancelled classes for Monday as a precaution.
Over the course of Monday, the rain in Valencia and Alicante and on the Balearic Islands was expected to gradually ease and move further north into Catalonia.
Almost two years ago, the Valencia region was hit by a devastating flood disaster that killed more than 220 people.

articles.title: France sets curfews in parts of Paris, other cities after riots
articles.summary: French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said he instructed localized and "very limited" curfews in some areas after serious riots during protests in France, suggesting he had instr...
articles.full_text:
French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said he instructed localized and "very limited" curfews in some areas after serious riots during protests in France, suggesting he had instructed prefects to impose them as soon as Monday evening.
Lecornu said the curfews would be "partial" and "very locally limited" in scope, following a crisis meeting of the government.
Later, it was confirmed that authorities set curfews for parts of the capital, Paris, as well as cities such as Lille and Nice, as they faced pressure over security failings following a weekend of riots and looting stemming from nationwide anti-government protests.
At the weekend, protests against high living costs in France were accompanied by riots and looting. The situation remained tense as the new week started, including in Paris.
The prime minister said that the "chaos" was limited to city centers and that the situation was "geographically very uneven."
"One of the aims of this curfew is the protection of people, but also of property, in particular shops," Lecornu said.
He said authorities were dealing with a specific form of criminal activity involving looting and the resale of stolen goods.
Lecornu did not rule out declaring a state of emergency but said such a serious measure was not appropriate at this stage, with targeted curfews better suited to the situation.
The instructions come as Interior Minister Laurent Nunez offered his resignation Sunday, but President Emmanuel Macron refused it "given the need for continued command of law enforcement in the current context," Macron's office said in a statement Monday.
He instructed Nunez "to take all necessary steps to ensure full transparency about the failures in planning and intelligence-gathering that led to the violence," the statement said.
Macron also asked for the introduction of "new policing tactics on the ground as quickly as possible" to put an end to violent events.
Meanwhile, France's "Yellow Vest" protest movement has announced further demonstrations for Saturday, Oct. 24.
Organizers of last weekend's rallies said on their website that a "second act" of the protests would take place in dozens of locations across the country.
The Yellow Vest movement, which takes its name from the high-visibility vests worn by demonstrators, staged months of protests against the high cost of living and social inequality from November 2018 into early 2019.
Calls to revive the movement emerged ahead of last weekend's demonstrations, which also drawing in Yellow Vest protesters.
The world-famous Louvre art museum in Paris did not open as usual at the start of the week due to the student protest movement, the museum said on its website and on social media on Monday morning.
The museum apologized for "the inconvenience caused."
French media reported that students blocked access to the museum to support the school protests that have been taking place for weeks and to denounce alleged police violence.
The French CGT union, which is not taking part in the action but supports it, originally said the museum should remain closed until at least midday, but the Louvre issued an update later to say it would remain closed all day.
Pupils have been demonstrating since late September, particularly for better school equipment, more teachers and better learning conditions.
Monday also marks the anniversary of the spectacular break-in at the Louvre, in which French crown jewels worth an estimated 88 million euros ($99 million) was stolen.
Later during the day, Paris police issued an overnight curfew in two areas of the French capital in efforts to prevent further violence.
The order aims to protect "people and property from the violence and looting," the Paris police statement said.
The curfew prohibits anyone from entering or remaining on the Place de la République, where rioting took place Saturday, and the shopping neighborhood of Les Halles, which has been subject to looting.
The curfew will be in effect from 11 p.m. Monday until 6 a.m. Tuesday. In addition, gatherings and demonstrations are banned from 8 p.m., the Paris police said.
In northern France, local authorities imposed a curfew for children and teenagers under the age of 18 in several cities, including Lille, starting from Monday and for the next two days from 8 p.m. to 6 a.m.
Nice, on the French Riviera, also imposed an overnight curfew for minors from 9 p.m.
Meanwhile, some European governments on Monday advised citizens travelling to France to avoid large crowds and exercise caution, warning of a deterioration in security conditions after thousands were arrested and shops looted in protests over the weekend.
Italy said its citizens should register their presence in France on a website or an app to enable them to be located, as it warned them to avoid large crowds and exercise extreme caution.
The German foreign ministry said further riots in the coming days couldn't be ruled out and urged German nationals to follow instructions from local police. It warned citizens that they could face fines or claims for damages if they failed to leave unauthorised demonstrations when asked to do so.
Czechs in France were also advised to avoid demonstrations, marches and public gatherings, CTK news agency reported. The security situation in France has deteriorated, according to the Czech foreign affairs ministry.
Other countries, including Poland, the Netherlands and Nordic nations, have also issued advisories.

articles.title: Albania's Rama warns protesters after police station set ablaze
articles.summary: Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama said Monday that anti-government demonstrators had crossed a "red line" after a police station was set on fire during protests. Demonstrators have...
articles.full_text:
Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama said Monday that anti-government demonstrators had crossed a "red line" after a police station was set on fire during protests.
Demonstrators have clashed with police since Tuesday as months of protests escalate, driven by fresh demands for better university conditions, anger over corruption and renewed calls for Rama's resignation.
"Protests are a right, whereas violence is a crime; this red line must be drawn clearly at this critical stage of our democratic development," Rama said in a Facebook post.
The prime minister said he was prepared for dialogue, except with those who commit violence and political parties that fail to distance themselves from it.
Protesters again briefly clashed with police outside the education ministry on Monday afternoon, after gathering in their hundreds from early morning.
Demonstrators hurled stones at riot police, who responded with tear gas, forcing the crowd to disperse.
AFP reporters also saw a small group smashing the doors and windows of the appeals tribunal before police intervened, continuing the attacks on government buildings in recent days.
"We will continue our movement until Rama resigns. We are not criminals, we want social peace and better living conditions in our country," Leka Sina, a 22-year-old science student, told AFP.
"Violence is not a solution, but the government also needs to reflect deeply to understand this revolt," he added. Across the demonstrations police have regularly used water cannons, tear gas and rubber bullets to disperse crowds that have targeted government buildings and smashed stores in several parts of the city.
Protesters have hurled stones, petrol bombs and fireworks at police.
Around 300 people have been injured in the clashes, more than half of them police, according to the authorities.
Petrol bombs were thrown into a police station and the interior ministry entrance on Sunday.
Several other government buildings have been badly damaged in the demonstrations, including the education ministry, which remains a focal point of the demonstrations.
In a meeting with officers on Monday, Rama praised the police response and pledged a 2,500-euro ($2,200) payment to "each officer on the front lines" as well as a "significant salary increase" from Jan. 1.
Rama, who has blamed "foreign hands" for the unrest, also accused Iran and Russia of driving misinformation online.
Stressing that Russia is "not an ally of Albania," Rama warned against a "wave of Russian influence surging through the entire social media ecosystem".
He also warned against "tens of thousands of fake profiles," allegedly linked to Iran, which have been mobilised under the guise of environmental activism.
The anti-government protests in the Balkan nation were initially sparked by a controversial resort development linked to U.S. President Donald Trump's family.
