articles.title: Funding shortfall forces WFP to cut food aid to 500,000 Gazans
articles.summary: The World Food Programme said Monday it would end monthly assistance to 500,000 people in Gaza due to a funding shortfall, despite acute needs in the war-torn Palestinian territory...
articles.full_text:
The World Food Programme said Monday it would end monthly assistance to 500,000 people in Gaza due to a funding shortfall, despite acute needs in the war-torn Palestinian territory.
The cutbacks mean 1.1 million Palestinians in Gaza, about half the population, will receive either food or cash assistance each month from the U.N. agency in reduced amounts.
The WFP said its efforts mitigated the effects of a famine last year in Gaza – a description Israel disputed – and warned conditions had not improved enough to withdraw aid.
"People are not safe. Airstrikes continue daily. People remain displaced," Shaun Hughes, the WFP country director, told Agence France-Presse (AFP) in East Jerusalem.
"Almost everyone remains without a permanent home. The humanitarian conditions are brutal," he said.
Latest assessments show 1.4 million people, two-thirds of Gaza's population, are still "acutely food insecure" and need humanitarian aid to survive, he said.
Last August, the U.N.'s Integrated Food Security Phase Classification reported Gaza suffered famine conditions.
Israel, which has blockaded and waged a genocidal war on the territory since the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas incursion, described the finding as a lie.
The classification was lifted in December, two months after a U.S.-brokered cease-fire was announced in Gaza. Israel, however, has continued striking Gaza since then.
Since the cease-fire, the WFP stepped up assistance, reaching between 1.5 million and 1.8 million people monthly.
"This has been a lifeline. But now, rather than being able to sustain and scale up that assistance, we're actually having to reduce it," Hughes said.
"That's not because we don't have humanitarian access to deliver food; that's because we don't have funding."
In addition to reducing the number of ration recipients, the WFP also has reduced ration content.
Families receiving food assistance will now get one food parcel instead of two, along with a smaller bag of wheat flour, the WFP said in an operational note.
The 75,000 families receiving cash assistance will see amounts reduced from 1,250 to 750 shekels ($400 to $240) monthly.
The WFP is funded by governments and private donors. It has seen a sharp drop in resources, including when President Donald Trump's administration drastically slashed contributions to U.N. agencies and bilateral aid.
The agency says it needs about $450 million over the next six months for its operations in Gaza and the Israeli-occupied West Bank, but this year it has received only about half the usual funding for the Palestinian territories.
In September, the agency also halved the number of aid recipients in the West Bank, which Israel has occupied since 1967, from 400,000 to 200,000.
"Now is not the time in the history of Palestine and Gaza to turn away from what is happening in Gaza," Hughes said.
The WFP says conditions have moderately improved in Gaza but notes needs could rise again with the onset of winter.
Israel has allowed more goods into Gaza under the terms of a U.S.-brokered cease-fire but still imposes heavy restrictions, turning away shipments of anything with alleged military use – a policy that has included blocking even prosthetic limbs, the United Nations says.
Israel, meanwhile, has ramped up longstanding criticism of the United Nations since the Gaza war, accusing the world body of bias and perpetuating dependency among Palestinians.

articles.summary: At least 12 migrants drowned Monday in two separate incidents off the Greek islands of Lesbos and Samos after their boats capsized during coast guard pursuits, authorities said. Si...
articles.full_text:
At least 12 migrants drowned Monday in two separate incidents off the Greek islands of Lesbos and Samos after their boats capsized during coast guard pursuits, authorities said.
Six people died off Lesbos Monday after the collision, including a baby and four women, a coast guard official said.
A small boat carrying the other six victims – five men and a woman – capsized off Samos, the coast guard added. Rescuers saved 14 people from that boat, including an alleged Iranian organizer.
The Lesbos incident involved a speedboat carrying migrants colliding with the port side of a police patrol vessel, the official said. Eight people were rescued in that incident.
Authorities did not provide the nationalities of the victims or those rescued.
The Aegean Sea is a frequently used route for migrants traveling from Türkiye to Europe and has claimed many lives.
At least 15 migrants died in February off the Greek island of Chios after their boat collided with a coast guard patrol vessel.
One person died and 25 remain missing after a migrant boat sank off the island of Gavdos, near Crete, in September.
"Smugglers are putting migrants in grave danger," Migration Minister Thanos Plevris told Ertnews public broadcaster. Plevris, an advocate for strict migration policies, also praised the coast guard, saying, "They are doing everything they can to save lives while at the same time protecting our borders."
Greece is one of five European countries – with Austria, Denmark, Germany and the Netherlands – working to set up detention centers in Africa for migrants whose asylum claims have been rejected.
The initiative, however, lacks unanimous EU support, with notable opposition from France.
According to the EU Agency for Asylum, the 27 member states received 332,000 applications for international protection in the first half of this year, a 17% decrease from the same period last year as countries tighten migration policies.

President Emmanuel Macron acknowledged "failures in anticipation and intelligence" following violent protests in France but rejected Interior Minister Laurent Nunez's resignation, the presidential palace said Monday.
The protests follow weeks of student demonstrations that included street violence, rocking the country six months before its next presidential election and increasing pressure due to a weak economy and surging debt.
Fears of tensions within Macron's fragile government regarding apparent security shortcomings – coming as the government needs to pass a crucial budget bill to rein in its finances – could further unsettle investors.
Over the weekend, hundreds of thousands protested what many describe as declining and dysfunctional public services, leaving citizens to fend for themselves amid cost-of-living pressures.
In many cities, including Paris, Marseille and Lyon, rioters quickly hijacked peaceful protests, leading to vandalism and chaos.
Interior Minister Nunez told France Inter radio Saturday that France deployed 60,000 police and other security forces but acknowledged it was not enough to control violent crowds in some cities.
Macron's presidential office, the Elysee, said Monday that Nunez, a former Paris police chief, offered his resignation to the president following the riots.
Macron refused, but urged Nunez to urgently develop new strategies "to end the barricades and looting," the Elysee said.
It added that Nunez also needed to "ensure transparency regarding the failures in forecasting and intelligence that led to the violence."
Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin, a longtime Macron ally, echoed the president's calls Monday, telling France 2 television that intelligence failures left the state vulnerable in the face of what he called "extreme-left" rioters the state had underestimated.
Cost-of-living issues were also prominent during numerous protests in other European countries, including Italy, Belgium and Albania, over the weekend. High fuel prices, largely attributed to the conflict involving Iran, added to the burden for many.
In France, violent groups torched a town hall, pillaged shops and covered buildings in graffiti Saturday as they clashed with police throughout the country.
Clashes also broke out in Paris and Marseille Sunday, with riot police intervening to prevent attempts to ransack businesses.
A slide in bond prices pushed France's 10-year yield up 8 basis points to 4.86%, while Germany's 10-year yield, the benchmark for the eurozone, was flat at 3.41%.
"The modest recovery in French spreads over the past week will be tested Monday," Jim Reid, a Deutsche Bank analyst, said in a note.
French shares were also among the worst performers on the European market Monday, with the CAC 40 falling 1.3% in early trading. Shares of French banks BNP Paribas, Societe Generale and Credit Agricole each fell about 2%.

articles.title: Turkish ministers visit Belgium for critical EU talks, bilateral ties

articles.full_text:
Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan, Interior Minister Mustafa Çiftçi and Justice Minister Akın Gürlek were scheduled to depart for Belgium on Monday for a three-day visit. The delegation will hold talks with their Belgian counterparts, while Fidan will also meet with EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas and NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte.
The ministers will attend the fourth meeting of the Turkish-Belgian foreign, justice and interior ministers on Tuesday. The meeting will also be attended by Belgian Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Maxime Prévot, Interior Minister Bernard Quintin, Justice Minister Annelies Verlinden and Minister of Asylum, Migration, Integration and Urban Policy Anneleen Van Bossuyt.
The third meeting of the ministers was held in Ankara 10 years ago. The upcoming meeting will focus on bilateral cooperation in counterterrorism, the defense industry, consular and visa services, migration, judicial cooperation and law enforcement, Foreign Ministry sources said Monday. The ministers will also exchange views on regional and international issues.
Separately, Fidan will address an event at the European Policy Centre think tank and meet with representatives of the business community.
Foreign Ministry sources said increased mutual contacts between Türkiye and Belgium in recent years had helped develop and deepen bilateral cooperation in various fields. Most recently, Queen Mathilde visited Türkiye from May 10 to 14, 2026, on an economy-focused trip, accompanied by a delegation that included Belgium’s deputy prime minister and foreign minister, its minister of defense and foreign trade, and the prime ministers of the regional governments.
Trade volume between Türkiye and Belgium stood at $9.2 billion in 2025, with the two countries aiming to increase it to $15 billion. Earlier this month, Belgium hosted the EU-Türkiye Business Summit. Approximately 300,000 Turkish citizens living in Belgium serve as an important bridge between the two countries, the sources said.
The year 2026 has so far been fruitful for Turkish-Belgian relations, with nine defense-related agreements signed during high-level talks in Ankara.
